selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about any design choice: modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline in the space. It gives a reference point for the RNA modality. Later experiments can each change one factor against it: the encoder (scVI or scGPT, config_004 and config_007), the profile setting and aggregation (config_002 and config_003), or adding images (config_016). 3) With a limited budget and no prior information, a cheap and interpretable anchor gets the most out of every later comparison. Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several factors together and make the gains hard to attribute.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space as a reference point: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA RNA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464 as supporting evidence. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial baseline and cannot show whether the encoder, modality or profile setting helps or hurts performance. It is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation, or adding image features would improve on it. Its single-run variance is also unknown, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against it should treat small differences cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). We know nothing yet about how much signal the image modality carries, and image-based configurations make up most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal options). 2. Test: config_010 keeps everything else at its simplest (single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps RNA for images with a ResNet50 encoder. This gives a clean single-profile image baseline to compare directly with config_001 for the modality question. 3. Why now: establishing whether images are weaker, comparable or stronger than RNA is the highest-leverage uncertainty. It tells us whether to spend later budget on multimodal fusion and image-encoder comparisons (for example ResNet50 vs ViT-L), or to focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. Tuning RNA encoders or aggregation first would leave this larger structural question open.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile configuration with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion, as a first image baseline to compare against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), well below the RNA-only baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). This suggests that this particular image setup carries less class-relevant signal than PCA-encoded RNA. However, the two runs differ in both modality and encoder, so the gap cannot be attributed to the image modality alone rather than to ResNet50 features specifically. It also remains unknown whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA would make image features useful (the latter as complementary rather than redundant information), and single-run variance has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only two single-profile baselines exist. RNA-only PCA reached 0.485 accuracy (F1 0.464), and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.208 (F1 0.172). So RNA is currently the stronger modality. Whether multiprofile input with aggregation helps is completely untested, even though that choice applies to most remaining configurations, across both modalities and fusion. 2. Test: This keeps the strongest baseline fixed (RNA-only, PCA encoder) and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). That isolates whether combining multiple profiles adds class-relevant signal. 3. Why now: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the best result so far. A gain would point to a broadly applicable direction and justify trying transformer aggregation next. No gain would let us deprioritize many multiprofile configurations. Either outcome cuts uncertainty about a high-impact design choice before we spend budget on encoder or fusion variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 was a one-factor comparison against the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) baseline (llm_summary_001), changing only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, making this the best result so far and suggesting that pooling multiple profiles adds class-relevant signal for PCA-encoded RNA. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, the gain cannot yet be split between them, and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, though a gain of about 0.1 is unlikely to be noise alone. Several questions remain untested: whether the benefit carries over to image-only or fusion settings and to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), and whether richer aggregation (e.g., transformer) improves on avgpool.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA multiprofile run with avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat its single-profile counterpart (0.485 acc). That makes multiprofile input the strongest direction so far. Because multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, it is still unknown how much the aggregation method matters. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), so adding fusion now is lower priority. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best run fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether a learned set aggregator extracts more signal from multiple profiles than simple averaging. 3) Value: aggregation is a choice shared by every remaining multiprofile configuration, across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings. Resolving it now builds on the strongest evidence and prunes a large part of the search space. Comparing encoders (scVI, scGPT) or adding fusion can then use the better aggregator. Any small difference should be read alongside F1, given unmeasured run-to-run variance.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was a one-factor comparison against the best run so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile). It changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer set aggregator. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.480, which suggests that, in this setting and with this configuration, transformer aggregation underperforms simple averaging; it still stays slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1), weakly hinting that multiprofile input helps somewhat even without avgpool. The result comes from a single run with unmeasured variance, and it is unknown whether the transformer was limited by training budget, hyperparameters or data size, or whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only or fusion settings, so avgpool is the provisionally preferred aggregator rather than a confirmed one.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The ResNet50 image-only baseline was weak (0.208), so adding images is not an obvious win. The RNA encoder choice is still completely untested, and all RNA results so far use PCA. 2) This experiment keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It tests whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation improves on PCA. 3) The encoder choice affects every RNA-only and multimodal configuration, so this answer narrows a large part of the remaining search space. The comparison is a clean one-factor test against the current best. It is also a plausible candidate to set a new best, which balances exploration and exploitation better than testing fusion with weak image features.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was a one-factor comparison against the previous best (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, PCA-2000), changing only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628, making this the new best configuration. Because only the encoder changed, this suggests that the scVI-200 representation is more useful than PCA-2000 in this setting. However, scVI differs from PCA in both being learned and being lower-dimensional, so the gain cannot be attributed to either property alone. Several points remain uncertain: the result comes from a single run with unmeasured variance (though a gain of about 0.06 is moderately large); it is untested whether the encoder advantage holds for single-profile, transformer aggregation or fusion settings, or how scVI compares with scGPT; and whether adding image features to this stronger RNA representation would help is still unknown, given the weak ResNet50 image-only baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: In the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting, the RNA encoder has had a large effect. Switching from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (F1 0.573 to 0.628), the best result so far. Avgpool has been provisionally preferred over the transformer aggregator. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, so the encoder ranking is still incomplete. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the encoder from scVI-200 to scGPT, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats or trails scVI. It finishes the encoder comparison in the strongest known setting, and it may also produce a new best configuration. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Every multimodal configuration depends on choosing an RNA backbone. Image signal has so far been weak (0.208 accuracy with ResNet50). Settling the RNA encoder first means later fusion experiments can be anchored on the strongest RNA representation, which avoids spending budget on multimodal runs built on a suboptimal encoder. It is a clean one-factor test that mixes exploitation and exploration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the best run (llm_summary_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, scVI-200), switching from scVI-200 to scGPT, which completes the RNA encoder comparison in this setting. Validation accuracy fell to 0.530 (F1 0.515), below both scVI-200 (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) and PCA-2000 (llm_summary_003: 0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) under the same settings, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485). This gives a provisional encoder ranking for this setting of scVI-200 > PCA-2000 > scGPT, which supports anchoring later fusion experiments on scVI-200. It remains uncertain why scGPT underperformed (e.g., how its embeddings were extracted or adapted, dimensionality, or training budget), whether the ranking holds for single-profile, transformer-aggregation or fusion settings, and how large single-run variance is, so the ranking should be treated as preliminary rather than confirmed.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: all RNA-only runs are informative but not settled. Multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). scVI-200 is the best RNA encoder so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1, ahead of PCA and scGPT). The main untested question is whether adding image features helps at all. The only image evidence is a weak single-profile ResNet50 image-only run (0.208), which cannot show whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only one thing: ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. The comparison with config_005 therefore isolates the effect of adding the image modality. ResNet50 is used rather than ViT-L so that the image encoder is the one we already have a baseline for, and concat is the simplest fusion reference. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest configuration while testing the central design choice in the study, multimodal versus unimodal. Either outcome guides the remaining budget. A gain would justify exploring image encoders and fusion types. No gain or a drop would suggest putting effort into RNA-side refinements or testing ViT-L features first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor comparison against the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: multiprofile, avgpool, scVI-200). The only change was adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion, which tests whether the image modality adds complementary signal. Validation accuracy fell slightly from 0.650 to 0.632 and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607, so in this setup adding ResNet50 features via concat gave no benefit and may have slightly hurt. Both values still exceed every other run, including PCA-2000 multiprofile (0.591). The drop of about 0.02 is small and comes from single runs with unmeasured variance, so it may be noise rather than a real degradation. It is also unknown whether the null result reflects the image modality itself, the weak ResNet50 features (image-only reached only 0.208), the simple concat fusion, or untuned training. Other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and other fusion methods therefore remain untested before multimodal fusion can be judged unhelpful.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.650 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered accuracy to 0.632. That null result is ambiguous. ResNet50 features look weak (image-only accuracy was 0.208), so we cannot tell whether the image modality adds nothing or whether this particular encoder is the problem. 2. What this tests: config_036 changes only the image encoder relative to config_030, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Everything else stays the same: scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. This isolates whether a stronger image representation can add signal that complements the strong RNA setup. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder is the largest untested factor and the most likely cause of the failed fusion. Testing fusion method first (weighted, config_031) with the same weak ResNet50 features would be less decisive. This run either uncovers a multimodal gain above 0.650 or makes it more credible that the image modality adds little, which would guide how much of the remaining budget to spend on multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor comparison against llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, avgpool, concat fusion), changing only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.715 and F1 from 0.607 to 0.687, making this the new best configuration and the first multimodal run to exceed the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). This suggests that, in this setting, the ViT-L image representation adds signal that complements scVI-200 RNA features, and that the earlier null fusion result was more likely tied to the ResNet50 features than to the image modality itself. It remains uncertain how much of the gain comes from ViT-L features alone versus their complementarity with RNA, because no ViT-L image-only baseline exists; whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) or aggregators would add further gains; and how large single-run variance is, though a gain of about 0.06–0.08 is moderately large.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best run so far is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Earlier single-factor comparisons favoured multiprofile over single-profile, avgpool over transformer, scVI-200 over PCA and scGPT, and ViT-L over ResNet50. Fusion is the only design axis never tested: every multimodal run used concat, so we don't know whether concat is limiting the gain from adding images. 2) This run changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, keeping everything else as in config_036. It shows whether a learned weighting of the two modalities adds to the RNA–image complementarity seen with ViT-L. The result is useful either way: a gain extends the best setup, and a drop or tie supports concat as the default. 3) It explores an untested factor while building on the strongest configuration, so it has a good chance of an immediate improvement. A ViT-L image-only baseline (config_014) would help explain where the multimodal gain comes from, but it is unlikely to beat the current best. Settling the fusion choice first is the better use of limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor comparison against the current best run (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted. It was the first test of the fusion axis, since all earlier multimodal runs used concat. Validation accuracy was 0.706 versus 0.715, and F1 was 0.667 versus 0.687, so weighted fusion did not improve on concat and was slightly worse, especially on F1. It still exceeded the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: 0.650 accuracy). This makes concat the provisional default fusion choice, but the gap (about 0.009 accuracy and 0.02 F1) is small and comes from single runs with unmeasured variance, so it may be a tie rather than a real disadvantage. It also remains unknown whether weighted fusion was limited by tuning or training budget, whether the fusion ranking holds with other encoders or aggregators, and how much of the multimodal gain comes from ViT-L features alone, since no ViT-L image-only baseline has been run.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best run is config_036 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Weighted fusion (config_037) roughly tied it. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised multimodal accuracy by about 0.08. We still cannot tell whether that gain reflects true complementarity with RNA or simply that ViT-L image features are strong on their own, because the only image-only baseline is ResNet50 single-profile (0.208). 2) What this tests: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile and avgpool, so it differs from config_036 only by removing the RNA branch. Comparing it with config_036 (0.715) and the scVI RNA-only run config_005 (0.650) shows how much each modality contributes and whether fusion is additive or redundant. It also tests whether the multiprofile and avgpool benefit seen for RNA carries over to images. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: This uncertainty has been flagged repeatedly and bears on how to read every multimodal result. A single clean ablation reduces it. It is more informative than exploiting nearby variants of the best configuration, such as transformer aggregation, which has already underperformed avgpool for RNA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was a modality ablation of the current best run (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat, 0.715 accuracy). It removed only the RNA branch, giving an image-only ViT-L multiprofile avgpool model, which reached 0.332 validation accuracy (F1 0.315). That is far below both the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005, scVI-200: 0.650) and the multimodal best (0.715), so ViT-L features alone carry only modest class signal and cannot by themselves explain the multimodal result. This is consistent with the roughly 0.065 multimodal gain over RNA-only reflecting complementary image information on top of RNA, rather than strong standalone image features. The run also improves on the only other image-only run (llm_summary_002, ResNet50 single-profile: 0.208), but that comparison changes both the encoder and the profile/aggregation setting, so it remains untested how much comes from ViT-L versus multiprofile avgpool for images. All results are single runs with unmeasured variance, which matters most for the small multimodal margins.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against by changing one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), or adding an image modality and fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, an anchor baseline makes every later result interpretable as the effect of a single design choice. Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would mix several factors together and prevent attributing gains, so the cheap, interpretable baseline is the best first experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because this is the first completed experiment, the result is only an initial reference point. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multi-profile aggregation, or adding the image modality with fusion would help or hurt. Its main value is as an anchor for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. Its variance across seeds or splits is also unknown, so small differences in future runs should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment is complete. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We have no evidence yet on the main design axes: profile setting, RNA encoder, image modality, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: Profile setting splits the search space roughly in half, since most remaining configurations are multi-profile. Its effect is likely to carry over to image-only and multimodal models. A clean one-factor comparison against config_001 will tell us whether to focus on multi-profile variants and whether to test transformer aggregation next. Encoder and modality comparisons (config_004, config_010) remain the natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only model and PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder from llm_summary_001 fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (+~0.106), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (+~0.109). Because this is a close one-factor comparison, the gain plausibly reflects moving to multi-profile input, but multi-profile and avgpool aggregation change together, so their separate contributions are unknown. Each result comes from a single run with unknown seed/split variance, and it remains untested whether the benefit holds for other aggregations (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders, or image-only and multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In the RNA-only PCA setting, moving from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with a similar F1 gain. That is the strongest signal so far. However, profile setting and aggregation changed together, so we do not know whether the gain comes from multiple profiles or from avgpool specifically. 2. Test: config_003 keeps config_002 identical (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multi-profile) and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the aggregation choice. It shows whether a learned aggregator adds value or whether simple pooling is enough. 3. Why now: This builds on the most promising direction with a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation also applies to almost every remaining multi-profile configuration, unimodal and multimodal alike, so settling it early can prune much of the search space. Encoder and modality questions can follow once the multi-profile setup is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept llm_summary_002 fixed (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, so this is a clean one-factor comparison of aggregation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (about -0.072), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (about -0.093). This suggests that in this setting the transformer aggregator underperformed simple average pooling, though it stayed modestly above the single-profile baseline (accuracy 0.4849, F1 0.4639). That hints that part of the multi-profile benefit may hold across aggregators, but it does not separate the profile and aggregation effects. Each result comes from a single run with unknown seed and split variance, and the transformer's capacity and training settings may not have been tuned, so it remains uncertain whether learned aggregation is truly worse or just under-optimized, and whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only models, or multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: In the clean comparisons so far, multi-profile input with avgpool aggregation is the strongest setting (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open design question for a multimodal study. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (PCA n2000, multi-profile, avgpool) and adds a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Concat is the minimal fusion choice. The result shows directly whether image features add useful signal on top of the best configuration, or whether they hurt it. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest direction found so far and resolves the most consequential uncertainty in a single run. A gain would point the search toward multimodal configurations, and the image-encoder and fusion variants could then be tested one at a time. No gain would suggest focusing on RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT. This is a one-step change from config_002, so it is easy to interpret, although results are single runs and small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion, making the model multimodal. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (about +0.028), and supporting F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (about +0.038), making this the best configuration so far and an initial sign that image features may add useful signal on top of RNA. The gain is modest and comes from single runs with unknown seed and split variance, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. Adding the image encoder and the concat fusion changed together, so their separate roles are not isolated. It also remains untested how an image-only model performs, whether other image encoders or fusion methods do better, and whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multi-profile input with avgpool clearly helped the RNA-only model (0.485 to 0.591). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a further modest gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). That gain is small, comes from single runs, and the image modality has never been tested alone, so we do not know how much signal images carry. 2) What this tests: An image-only, multi-profile ResNet50 model with avgpool matches config_018 except that RNA is removed. Together with config_002, which removes the image side, it brackets the multimodal result. If image-only is weak, images are a minor complement to RNA. If it is near or above 0.62, images drive much of the performance, and the fusion design or image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) deserves priority. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It answers a basic question about how much each modality contributes, which will guide whether later budget goes to RNA encoders, image encoders or fusion methods. Testing those directly now would build on an unverified assumption about where the useful signal comes from.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an image-only model (ResNet50, multi-profile, avgpool, no RNA or fusion), matching llm_summary_004 except that the RNA side was removed and serving as the image counterpart to the RNA-only llm_summary_002. It reached validation accuracy 0.3275 (supporting F1 0.2884), far below RNA-only multi-profile (0.5907), the multimodal model (0.6186), and even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.4849). This suggests that in this setup ResNet50 image features alone carry much less discriminative signal than RNA, and that RNA likely drives most of the multimodal performance, with images at most a minor complement. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and the image encoder was not varied, so a weak ResNet50 representation or untuned image training cannot be ruled out (ViT-L is untested). It is also unclear whether the small multimodal gain in llm_summary_004 reflects real complementary image signal or noise.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only reached 0.328, and adding ResNet50 images gave only about +0.028 (0.619), which may be within noise. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best RNA setting so far, beating both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Yet every run used the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the RNA representation is the largest untested design choice for the dominant modality. 2) Test: config_005 swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI (n200) and keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, no image). Compared with config_002, this cleanly isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Why now: because RNA dominates, the RNA encoder choice is likely to shift performance more than image encoder or fusion tweaks. The result will guide whether later multimodal runs should use PCA or scVI, or should next test scGPT. That makes it the best use of the next experiment under a limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multi-profile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200, a clean one-factor test of the RNA representation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 (about +0.059), and supporting F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6275 (about +0.055). This RNA-only run is now the best configuration so far, above the PCA-based multimodal model llm_summary_004 (0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1). This suggests the scVI representation helps in this setting and that the RNA encoder may matter more than adding ResNet50 images. Results are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and scVI differs from PCA in both method and dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so these two factors cannot be separated. It also remains untested whether the gain carries over to multimodal fusion, other aggregators, or other encoders such as scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.328, while RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591 with PCA. Changing the RNA encoder was one of the largest effects so far: switching PCA to scVI within the same RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup gave +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1, making config_005 the best result (0.650). Adding ResNet50 images gave only a modest, possibly noisy gain (+0.028). The third RNA encoder option, scGPT, is completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best known setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor comparison that completes the encoder axis (PCA vs scVI vs scGPT) under identical conditions. 3) The encoder appears to be the most important design choice, so knowing which encoder is best should come before multimodal fusion tests. Every later multimodal or fusion experiment depends on that choice. If scGPT beats scVI, the search should pivot to scGPT-based multimodal configurations. If it does not, scVI is confirmed as the base for testing whether images add value (e.g., config_030). Either outcome directly narrows the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup fixed (multi-profile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder to scGPT, completing a one-factor comparison of the three RNA encoders. It reached validation accuracy 0.5305 (supporting F1 0.5152), well below scVI n=200 (0.6501 / 0.6275; about -0.120 accuracy) and also below PCA n=2000 (0.5907 / 0.5727; about -0.060), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This suggests that in this setup scGPT embeddings are the weakest of the three RNA representations and supports scVI as the base for later multimodal and fusion tests. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and scGPT likely differs from the others in embedding dimensionality, pretraining domain, gene-vocabulary coverage, and possibly preprocessing, so it remains uncertain whether its gap reflects an inherently weaker representation or an untuned or mismatched integration, and whether the ranking holds in multimodal or other-aggregator settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI n=200 with multi-profile avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). With the PCA encoder, adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion gave a modest gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). However, image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), so it is unclear whether that gain is real complementary signal or noise, and whether it survives with a stronger RNA representation. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (scVI, multi-profile, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image encoder with concat fusion. It is a clean replication of the image-addition effect on a second RNA backbone. If the gain holds, multimodal fusion is supported. If it shrinks or reverses, images may only help weaker RNA encoders. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it is both exploitation and a clean test. It is the most likely candidate to beat the current best, and it answers whether the multimodal direction deserves further budget. That answer should come before spending runs on other image encoders (ViT-L), weighted fusion, or transformer aggregation, which was clearly worse than avgpool with PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_006 fixed (multi-profile, scVI n=200, avgpool) and added only a ResNet50 image encoder with concat fusion, replicating on a second RNA backbone the image-addition test from llm_summary_004. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6501 to 0.6315 (about -0.019), and supporting F1 fell from 0.6275 to 0.6068 (about -0.021), so the RNA-only scVI model remains the best configuration. This contrasts with the +0.028 accuracy gain seen when images were added to PCA, which suggests the earlier gain may not be robust, or that ResNet50 images help only weaker RNA representations; the result fits the weak image-only performance (0.3275). All results are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and both differences (+0.028 and -0.019) are small enough to fall within noise; in addition, image addition and concat fusion change together, so it remains uncertain whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or a different fusion method could make images complementary to scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI RNA-only (multi-profile, avgpool) is the best result so far (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave +0.028 on the PCA backbone but -0.019 on the scVI backbone. ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.328). The main open question is whether images are weak in this task or only weakly represented by ResNet50, because the image encoder has never been varied. 2) Test: config_036 differs from config_030 only in the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L). It keeps scVI, multi-profile, avgpool and concat fixed, so it cleanly isolates the effect of image representation on the strongest RNA backbone. If ViT-L beats scVI RNA-only, images are complementary and the search should pursue multimodal configurations. If it does not, the evidence that RNA alone suffices gets stronger. 3) Why now: it reduces the largest remaining uncertainty, image representation quality, while also being a plausible candidate for a new best. Testing weighted fusion (config_031) or ViT-L image-only (config_014) would be less direct. Fusion tuning matters little if the image features themselves carry little signal.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept llm_summary_008 fixed (multimodal, multi-profile, scVI n=200, avgpool, concat) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, a clean one-factor test of image representation on the strongest RNA backbone. Validation accuracy rose to 0.7150 (supporting F1 0.6872), about +0.084 over the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.6315 / 0.6068) and about +0.065 over the previous best, scVI RNA-only (0.6501 / 0.6275), making it the new best configuration. This suggests the earlier weak image contribution likely reflected a limited ResNet50 representation rather than images lacking signal, and that ViT-L image features may be complementary to scVI RNA. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, but the gain is larger than earlier differences (about ±0.02–0.03). ViT-L image-only performance is untested, so its standalone signal is unknown. It is also unknown whether the benefit holds with PCA or other RNA encoders, or with other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) or aggregators. ViT-L may also differ from ResNet50 in feature dimensionality and capacity, so which property drives the gain is not isolated.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n=200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is clearly the best so far at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. That is about +0.065 over scVI RNA-only, a larger gap than earlier differences of roughly ±0.02 to 0.03. The other choices already have one-factor evidence: multiprofile beat singleprofile, avgpool beat transformer, scVI beat PCA and scGPT, and ViT-L beat ResNet50. Fusion is the one design choice never tested; every multimodal run used concat. 2) Test: config_037 changes only concat to weighted fusion on the best setup. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest backbone. It also checks whether a learned weighting of RNA and image features can extract more from the ViT-L signal. 3) Why now: it exploits the strong ViT-L+scVI direction while closing the largest remaining knowledge gap. A ViT-L image-only run would mainly be diagnostic and is unlikely to improve accuracy. A transformer-aggregation run is lower priority because transformer aggregation already underperformed once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration, llm_summary_009 (multimodal, multi-profile, scVI n=200, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool), fixed and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. This was the first test of fusion, since every earlier multimodal run used concat. Validation accuracy was 0.7062 (supporting F1 0.6671), slightly below concat (0.7150 / 0.6872; about -0.009 accuracy, -0.020 F1) but still well above scVI RNA-only (0.6501) and the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.6315). So weighted fusion gave no gain on this backbone, concat remains the best, and the strong ViT-L+scVI result appears fairly robust to the fusion choice. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and the accuracy gap is smaller than earlier differences of about ±0.02–0.03, so the two fusion methods may be equivalent within noise. It also remains untested whether weighted fusion behaves differently with other encoders or aggregators, or whether its weighting scheme or training settings were under-tuned.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2) config_001 is the simplest reference point: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a baseline accuracy and F1 against which each design choice can later be compared one factor at a time, for example RNA encoder (config_004 or config_007), profile setting (config_002), image-only (config_010), and adding fusion (config_016). 3) Starting with an interpretable, low-complexity baseline is the best first use of the budget. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and every later experiment becomes a controlled single-factor comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest reference configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.464. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial baseline. It says nothing yet about whether modality, RNA encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. Those effects remain unknown until controlled single-factor comparisons are run against this baseline, for example an alternative RNA encoder, a multiprofile setting, an image-only model, or added fusion. How much the result varies across runs is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only one experiment is complete, the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). There is no evidence yet on modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) What this tests: config_002 keeps the RNA-only model and the PCA-2000 encoder and changes only the profile setting from single to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps on its own, without the added complexity of a transformer aggregator. 3) Why now: profile setting applies across most of the remaining search space (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings). Learning its effect early will shape how the rest of the limited budget is spent. Avgpool gives a clean answer on profile setting before transformer aggregation is tried. A follow-up experiment can then test an alternative RNA encoder or adding images with the same controlled single-factor approach.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 configuration from baseline llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573 (+0.109). This suggests that, in this RNA-only PCA-2000 setting, multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation outperforms single-profile input. Several points remain uncertain: the comparison rests on one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance; the gain cannot be attributed to having multiple profiles separately from the avgpool choice, since the two changed together; and it is unknown whether the effect holds for other aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders, or image-only and multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: moving the RNA-only PCA-2000 model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool improved validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 moved by a similar amount. This is the clearest signal so far, though it comes from one run each. It is still unclear how much of the gain comes from using multiple profiles and how much from the aggregation choice. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. That isolates the effect of the aggregator. It shows whether the multiprofile benefit holds with a learned aggregator, and whether that aggregator adds value or overfits compared with simple averaging. 3) Aggregation applies to every later multiprofile experiment, including the RNA-encoder, image-only and multimodal ones. Settling it now with a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest result narrows the search space efficiently. It also exploits the promising multiprofile direction rather than switching several factors at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (-0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.480 (-0.093). In this setting, the transformer aggregator therefore underperformed simple averaging, though it still scored slightly above the single-profile baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown; it is unclear whether the drop reflects overfitting, insufficient tuning or training of the transformer, or a real limitation of the aggregator; and it is unknown whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders or for image-only and multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far covers only RNA-only PCA-2000 models. Multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 acc / 0.573 F1) clearly beat single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519), though each result comes from a single run. Whether image data adds anything is completely untested, and modality is arguably the most consequential design choice in this study. 2) Config_018 keeps the best-known setup fixed (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This tests whether combining modalities improves on the strongest RNA-only model. Adding images requires some fusion method, so concat is the minimal change. 3) This is a controlled extension of the strongest direction, so it is useful whichever way it turns out. If it helps, it opens the multimodal branch for follow-up on the image encoder and fusion choice. If it does not, it argues for focusing the budget on RNA-encoder comparisons such as config_005 or config_008. Either result tells us more than an RNA-encoder swap would, because the encoder can be tested afterwards within whichever modality setting proves better.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion, making it the first multimodal configuration tested. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (+0.028) and validation F1 rose from 0.573 to 0.610 (+0.038), the best result so far. This is an initial indication that adding image data via simple concatenation may help, though the gain is smaller than the multiprofile gain seen earlier (+0.106 accuracy). Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so a gain of this size may not be robust. The effect of adding images also cannot be separated from the specific choices of ResNet50 encoder and concat fusion, and no image-only model has been run to show how much the image branch contributes on its own. It is also unknown whether the benefit holds for other RNA encoders, aggregators, or fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input with avgpool clearly helped the RNA-only model (+0.106 accuracy over single-profile). The transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool. Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_018) gave the best result so far, 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That gain was modest (+0.028) and comes from single runs, and no image-only model has been run. So it is unknown how much of the multimodal result comes from images versus RNA. 2. What this tests: config_011 is the image-only counterpart of config_018, with the same multiprofile setting, avgpool aggregation and ResNet50 encoder, and the RNA branch removed. It completes a clean ablation. If image-only is close to or above 0.619, the RNA branch or concat fusion adds little and the search should focus on image encoders. If it is well below, fusion is doing real work and testing fusion type or RNA encoder becomes the priority. 3. Why now: It isolates the modality question with a single-factor change from the best configuration. Its result will guide the next tests: alternative image encoders such as ViT-L, alternative RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT, or weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an image-only ResNet50 model with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation. It is the image-only counterpart of the best multimodal configuration (llm_summary_004), with the RNA branch removed as a single-factor ablation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 (F1 0.288). That is far below the multimodal result (0.619 / 0.610), the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.591 / 0.573), and even the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This suggests that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features alone carry much weaker label-relevant signal than PCA-2000 RNA features, and that the RNA branch supplies most of the multimodal performance. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run with unknown variance, and chance-level accuracy is not given, so it is unclear how informative the image features are in absolute terms. The image branch's added value within the multimodal model still rests only on the modest +0.028 gain over RNA-only. It is also unknown whether a different image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), aggregator, or fusion method (e.g., weighted fusion) would change the image contribution.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is the dominant signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, adding ResNet50 images raised this only modestly to 0.619, and image-only reached just 0.328. Multiprofile input with avgpool was the largest gain so far (+0.106 over single-profile), while the transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool. However, every result so far uses PCA-2000, so the RNA encoder choice is completely untested even though it likely governs most of the performance. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This is a clean single-factor comparison with config_002 that shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation improves the strongest modality. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: because RNA drives the results, a better RNA representation is likely to matter more than smaller adjustments to the weak image branch or the fusion method. The result also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal experiments, so it guides most of the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT, giving a clean single-factor test of a pretrained foundation-model representation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.530 (-0.060) and validation F1 fell from 0.573 to 0.515 (-0.057). This suggests that in this setting scGPT embeddings underperform PCA-2000, although scGPT still beat the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464), so PCA-2000 currently looks like the stronger RNA encoder to carry forward. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run with unknown variance, and it is unclear whether the drop reflects the scGPT representation itself or choices such as frozen versus fine-tuned use, embedding dimensionality, or preprocessing compatibility. It is also unknown whether the ranking holds under other aggregators, single-profile input, or multimodal fusion with images.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, PCA-2000, ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That is a modest +0.028 over RNA-only. Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.328), so the image branch carries much less signal than RNA. Fusion method is the one design factor not yet tested at all, and concat may not handle a weak, noisy modality well. 2. Test: config_019 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, and keeps every other choice of the best configuration. This cleanly asks whether learned modality weighting makes better use of, or better down-weights, the weak image features. It also checks whether the multimodal gain holds up under a different fusion method. 3. Why now: it exploits the current best setup and resolves uncertainty about a previously unexplored design choice in a single-factor comparison. That is more informative per experiment than changing the encoder and fusion together. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L is a natural follow-up once the fusion choice is understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, multiprofile avgpool) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, as a single-factor test of fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.619 to 0.639 (+0.020) and validation F1 rose slightly from 0.610 to 0.620 (+0.009). This makes it the new best configuration and is an initial indication that weighted fusion may use the weak image branch (image-only 0.328) somewhat better than concatenation, with the multimodal advantage over RNA-only (0.591) holding under a second fusion method. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run with unknown variance, so gains of this size may not be robust, and the F1 gain is smaller than the accuracy gain. It is also unclear whether the learned weights actually down-weight the image modality or the gain comes from other properties of the fusion module, and it is unknown whether the ranking holds with a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Multiprofile avgpool and PCA-2000 have each beaten their alternatives once. The image branch is the weak link: ResNet50 image-only scored only 0.328 and added a modest +0.03 to +0.05 over RNA-only. The image encoder choice has never been tested, so whether a stronger image representation could raise the multimodal ceiling is a major open question. 2) Test: config_025 keeps the best configuration and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean single-factor test of image representation within the top-performing pipeline. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest current direction while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty about a design factor that could plausibly improve performance. Even a null or negative result is informative, because it would suggest the image modality's contribution is limited regardless of encoder. That would let later experiments focus on the RNA encoder (e.g., scVI) instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_007: multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, as a single-factor test of image representation. Validation accuracy was 0.635 versus 0.639 (-0.004), and validation F1 was 0.618 versus 0.620 (-0.001), so the swap gave no improvement. This initial observation suggests that, in this pipeline, a stronger general-purpose ImageNet encoder does not raise the multimodal ceiling, and llm_summary_007 remains the best configuration. Uncertainties: each configuration has one run with unknown variance, so the two encoders are effectively indistinguishable rather than ranked; no ViT-L image-only run exists to show whether its standalone signal differs from ResNet50 (0.328); and it is unknown whether domain-specific image encoders, fine-tuning, or other fusion and aggregation choices would change the image contribution, so the evidence is consistent with, but does not prove, a limited image contribution.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA supplies most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.328, RNA-only multiprofile 0.591, and the best multimodal config_019 reached 0.639. Weighted fusion beat concat slightly, and swapping the image encoder made no difference (0.635 vs 0.639). Among RNA encoders, PCA-2000 beat scGPT (0.591 vs 0.530). scVI-200 has never been tested, so it is the largest open question about the dominant modality. 2) What this tests: config_031 keeps everything from the current best config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It is a clean single-factor test of whether a probabilistic latent RNA representation beats PCA in the best-performing pipeline. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: the RNA representation is the most influential factor still unexplored, and testing it inside the top configuration serves both exploration and exploitation. If scVI wins, it could set a new best directly; if it loses, PCA-2000 is confirmed as the RNA encoder to carry forward, and later experiments can focus on secondary choices.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the previous best configuration (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, ResNet50 image encoder, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, a clean single-factor test of RNA representation in the dominant modality. Validation accuracy rose from 0.639 to 0.678 (+0.039) and validation F1 from 0.620 to 0.646 (+0.027), making this the new best configuration. This is an initial indication that the scVI-200 latent representation outperforms PCA-2000 within this pipeline, and the gain exceeds those from the fusion change (+0.020) and the image-encoder swap (-0.004). Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has only one run with unknown variance; there is no RNA-only scVI-200 run, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects a standalone RNA improvement or an interaction with weighted fusion and the image branch; and it is unknown whether the advantage holds under other fusion methods or aggregators, or with different scVI latent sizes or training settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The current best is config_031 (scVI-200 multimodal, weighted fusion, 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). It beat the PCA-2000 version by +0.039, the largest gain since adding multiprofile input. However, scVI has only been tested together with the image branch and weighted fusion. Images alone are weak (0.328), and they added only +0.02 to +0.05 on top of PCA RNA. So it is unclear whether scVI is a better standalone RNA representation or whether it interacts with fusion. 2) Test: config_005 is the RNA-only ablation of config_031 (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool). Compared with config_002 (PCA RNA-only, 0.591), it isolates the RNA-encoder effect without images or fusion. Compared with config_031, it measures how much the image branch adds under the stronger RNA encoder. That shows whether the multimodal benefit persists or shrinks when RNA is better. 3) Why now: RNA is the dominant modality, and the RNA encoder looks like the most important lever. This single-factor experiment clarifies two key design questions at once, the RNA representation and the value of multimodality. It is more informative than another incremental multimodal variant such as swapping in ViT-L, which earlier made no difference.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 ran an RNA-only scVI-200 model (multiprofile, avgpool). It differs from the PCA-2000 RNA-only run (llm_summary_002) only in the RNA encoder, and it is the RNA-only ablation of the current best multimodal configuration (llm_summary_009). It reached 0.650 validation accuracy (F1 0.628), +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over PCA-2000 RNA-only (0.591 / 0.573), and above even the best PCA multimodal result (0.639), so the scVI advantage appears to hold without images or fusion rather than depending only on the multimodal setup. Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (llm_summary_009, 0.678 / 0.646) still added +0.028 accuracy and +0.019 F1 over this run, an initial indication that a modest multimodal benefit persists with the stronger RNA encoder. That gain is similar to the PCA concat gain (+0.028) and somewhat below the PCA weighted-fusion gain (+0.048). Uncertainties: each configuration has one run with unknown variance, so differences of about 0.02 to 0.03 may not be robust; the encoder effect is confounded with representation dimensionality (200 vs 2000) and scVI training settings; and it is unknown whether the image contribution under scVI would differ with concat fusion, other aggregators, or other image encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) This experiment sets a simple baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA encoder, with no aggregation or fusion. Later experiments can each change one factor from it, such as swapping the RNA encoder for scVI or scGPT, switching to multiprofile with avgpool, adding image features, or comparing against an image-only baseline. That isolates the contribution of each design choice. 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap, low-variance reference point is the most informative first step. It gives every later, more complex configuration a fair comparison, rather than assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will win.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set a baseline using an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a validation F1 of 0.4639. The F1 is similar to the accuracy, which gives no strong sign of severe class imbalance effects, though this is not confirmed. No other experiments exist yet, so this is a reference point only, and the result cannot show whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choices matter. It is unknown how this baseline compares with alternatives such as scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion. Run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized, so small differences in future one-factor comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only one result exists, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We do not yet know which design choice matters most, and run-to-run variance is unknown. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the same modality and RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This gives a clean one-factor test of whether pooling several profiles improves accuracy over a single profile. 3. Why this one: Profile setting is a top-level choice that affects every branch of the search space, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal models. Using avgpool instead of a transformer avoids mixing in aggregator complexity. A clear gain would show that multiprofile variants deserve priority. No gain would steer the budget toward encoder or modality comparisons, such as scVI, scGPT or image-only models, as the next experiments.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only setting and the pca_n2000 RNA encoder from the baseline (llm_summary_001), but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average pooling, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (+0.106) and validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (+0.109). Because the profile setting and its required aggregation step changed together, the gain is attributable to the multiprofile+avgpool combination in this RNA-only PCA setting, not to multiprofile input or avgpool in isolation, and this initial evidence suggests multiprofile variants deserve priority. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run once and run-to-run variance is unknown, other aggregators (e.g., transformer) are untested, and it is unknown whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 (F1 0.464 to 0.573) in the RNA-only pca_n2000 setting. This is the only strong signal so far. Avgpool is the only aggregator tested, so we do not know whether the gain comes from multiprofile input alone or whether a learned aggregator would add more. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It extends the most promising direction with a single-factor change. The answer also shapes many remaining choices, because most untested multimodal and image configurations are multiprofile and must use one of the two aggregators. If the transformer clearly helps or hurts, later encoder, modality and fusion comparisons can focus on one aggregator and save budget. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image-only baselines are important but can follow once the aggregation choice is better understood.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to a transformer, isolating the effect of aggregation in this setting. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (-0.072), and validation F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (-0.093). This is an initial single-run observation that, in this RNA-only PCA setting, the transformer aggregator underperformed simple average pooling while still slightly exceeding the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy). The cause of the gap is not identified: run-to-run variance is unknown, and it is unclear whether the drop reflects the transformer itself or untuned training settings (e.g., capacity, regularization, number of profiles). It is also unknown whether this ranking of aggregators holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three runs so far are RNA-only with pca_n2000. Multiprofile with avgpool gave the best result (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beat single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The image modality is completely untested, which is the largest gap in our knowledge. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best setup (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a resnet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_002 isolates whether adding image information improves on the strongest RNA-only model. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a one-factor change from the current best configuration, so it both exploits the promising multiprofile+avgpool direction and probes the most important untested axis. Concat and resnet50 are the simplest fusion and image-encoder choices, so the result should be easy to interpret. If it improves on config_002, multimodal variants deserve priority. If not, an image-only run such as config_011 can tell whether the image features carry useful signal at all.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed one factor: it added a resnet50 image branch with concat fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (+0.028) and validation F1 from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (+0.038), the best result so far. Because only the image branch was added, this is initial single-run evidence that adding image information with this fusion helps in this setting. The gain is modest, though, and run-to-run variance is unknown, so it may be within noise. It is also unclear how much signal the image features carry alone (no image-only run yet, e.g., config_011), and whether other fusion methods, image encoders, RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or aggregators would change the result.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beat single-profile in the RNA-only PCA setting (+0.106 accuracy), and the transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool. Adding a resnet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_018) gave the best result so far, 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. That gain was modest (+0.028 accuracy) and came from a single run, so it may be within noise. We also have no measure of how much signal the images carry on their own. 2. What this tests: config_011 is the image-only counterpart of config_018, keeping multiprofile and avgpool fixed and dropping only the RNA branch. Together with config_002 (RNA-only) and config_018 (multimodal), it completes a matched modality comparison. If image-only is weak, the multimodal gain likely reflects complementary information or noise. If it is strong, or even beats multimodal, the RNA branch or the concat fusion may be adding little or interfering. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the modality question underlies every later choice, including whether to spend runs on image encoders (ViT-L), fusion types, or RNA encoders. Answering it now with a clean one-factor comparison is a better use of budget than tuning fusion or encoders around a gain that may not be real.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested an image-only, multiprofile model (resnet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, no RNA branch or fusion). It is the matched image-only counterpart of the multimodal run (llm_summary_004), which dropped only the RNA branch, and of the RNA-only run (llm_summary_002), which kept the same profile setting and aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 and validation F1 of 0.2884. This is far below RNA-only (0.5907 / 0.5727), the multimodal model (0.6186 / 0.6103), and even the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4849). The F1 falls further below accuracy here than in earlier runs, a possible but unconfirmed sign of uneven per-class performance. This initial single-run evidence suggests that, in this setting, resnet50 image features with avgpool carry much weaker signal alone than pca_n2000 RNA features. It also suggests RNA is the dominant modality. Image information may still add complementary value when fused, but the modest +0.028 multimodal gain cannot yet be separated from noise. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, and it is untested whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other aggregators, or other fusion methods would raise image-only performance or enlarge the multimodal benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA looks like the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with pca_n2000 reached 0.591 accuracy, against 0.328 for the matched image-only run. Adding resnet50 images gave only a modest, possibly-noise gain (0.619). Multiprofile with avgpool has clearly beaten single-profile and the transformer aggregator. The RNA encoder has never been varied, although it likely carries most of the predictive signal. 2) Test: config_005 keeps the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This is a clean one-factor test of whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3) Value: the RNA encoder probably matters more than the image encoder or fusion choice, and those effects look small so far. Resolving it in the cheaper RNA-only setting tells us which RNA backbone to carry into later multimodal and fusion experiments. If scVI helps, it is a direct path to better multimodal configs (e.g., config_030). If not, PCA is confirmed as the right backbone, and scGPT (config_008) remains to test.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multiprofile, avgpool, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, as a one-factor test of a learned latent representation against PCA. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 (+0.059) and validation F1 from 0.5727 to 0.6275 (+0.055). This is the best accuracy so far, above even the PCA-based multimodal run (llm_summary_004: 0.6186 accuracy / 0.6103 F1), though that run's F1 is nearly as high. This is initial single-run evidence that scVI is a stronger RNA backbone than PCA in this RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting, and that RNA encoder choice may matter more than adding resnet50 images. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown. The comparison also changes latent dimensionality (200 vs. 2000) along with the encoder type, so the gain cannot be attributed to the scVI method alone. It is also untested whether the benefit carries over to multimodal fusion (e.g., scVI plus resnet50 concat) or holds against scGPT and other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality. Image-only scored 0.328, against 0.591 for PCA RNA-only. Swapping the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI gave the largest one-factor gain so far (+0.059 accuracy, reaching 0.650 with F1 0.628). Adding resnet50 images to PCA gave only +0.028, which may be within noise. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup from config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. It isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats or matches scVI. 3) Encoder choice appears to be the most influential factor so far, and the winning RNA backbone shapes every later multimodal comparison. Resolving this uncertainty first avoids spending budget on fusion and image-encoder variants built on a suboptimal RNA encoder. Testing scVI plus images (config_030) remains the natural next exploitation step once the backbone is settled.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup used in llm_summary_002 (PCA) and llm_summary_006 (scVI) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, a one-factor test of a pretrained foundation-model representation against PCA and scVI. Validation accuracy was 0.5305 and F1 was 0.5152, well below scVI (0.6501 / 0.6275; -0.120 accuracy) and also below PCA (0.5907 / 0.5727; -0.060), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This is initial single-run evidence that, in this setting, scGPT is the weakest of the three RNA backbones tested and that scVI remains the preferred RNA encoder for later multimodal comparisons such as scVI plus images. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown. The cause of the gap is not isolated and could reflect how scGPT embeddings were extracted or adapted (frozen vs. fine-tuned, embedding dimensionality, gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch) rather than the representation itself. It is also untested whether scGPT would rank differently with other aggregators or in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is the RNA-only scVI model (config_005: multiprofile, avgpool), at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. With the PCA encoder, adding resnet50 images through concat fusion gave a modest gain (config_002 to config_018: +0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). That gain may be within noise, and image-only performance was weak (0.328). So it is still uncertain whether images add real complementary signal. 2. Test: config_030 adds the resnet50 image branch with concat fusion to config_005 and changes nothing else. It repeats the PCA image-addition comparison with the stronger scVI encoder. If both encoders show a gain, the evidence that fusion helps becomes stronger. If the gain disappears, the earlier improvement may have come from images compensating for weaker PCA features. 3. Value: This exploits the best-performing direction and has a realistic chance of a new best result. It also answers a central question, whether multimodal fusion helps, by changing only one factor. That makes it a better use of the budget than testing ViT-L or other fusion and aggregation variants first.
experiment_summary: This experiment added a resnet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_006: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed nothing else, repeating the one-factor image-addition test previously run with PCA (llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_004). Validation accuracy fell from 0.6501 to 0.6315 (-0.019) and F1 from 0.6275 to 0.6068 (-0.021), so scVI RNA-only remains the best configuration; the multimodal run edges the PCA multimodal run on accuracy (0.6186) but is slightly below it on F1 (0.6103). This is initial single-run evidence that the modest image gain seen with PCA (+0.028 accuracy) did not carry over to the stronger scVI encoder, which weakens the case that resnet50 concat fusion adds real complementary signal. It is consistent with the earlier gain reflecting images compensating for weaker PCA features or noise, though neither explanation is confirmed. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, both image-addition differences are small and may be within noise, and it is untested whether other fusion methods, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or tuning of the fused model (e.g., modality weighting or regularization) would change the result.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI RNA-only multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion lowered it slightly (0.632 / 0.607). Image-only resnet50 is weak (0.328), so images may be diluting the stronger RNA signal under naive concatenation. Fusion method is a major design choice that has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps everything from config_030 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. It tests whether learned modality weighting can use the weak image branch without hurting RNA performance, ideally recovering or exceeding the RNA-only result. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison on the strongest backbone, and both outcomes are informative. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, it gives a fusion strategy to carry into ViT-L runs. If it does not, it strengthens the conclusion that resnet50 images add little.
