Either way it guides how to spend the remaining budget on multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the scVI multimodal setup from llm_summary_008 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, as a one-factor test of whether learned modality weighting makes better use of the weak image branch (image-only resnet50: 0.3275 accuracy). Validation accuracy rose from 0.6315 to 0.6776 (+0.046) and F1 from 0.6068 to 0.6464 (+0.040). This is the best result so far, above scVI RNA-only (llm_summary_006: 0.6501 / 0.6275; +0.027 accuracy), which gives initial single-run evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in this setting and may let resnet50 images add modest value over RNA alone. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, so the gain over RNA-only is small and may be within noise. The learned modality weights were not reported, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects real image contribution or mainly reduced image interference. It is also untested whether weighted fusion helps with PCA or scGPT encoders, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other aggregators, or against other fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.6776 accuracy and 0.6464 F1. Its edge over scVI RNA-only (0.6501) is small and may be noise. Image-only resnet50 was weak (0.3275), so the image branch may be what limits the multimodal benefit. The image encoder choice has never been varied. 2. Test: This run keeps the best configuration and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to ViT-L. It shows whether stronger image features enlarge the multimodal gain under weighted fusion. 3. Value: It builds directly on the best result while answering a major open design question with a clean one-factor change. If ViT-L helps, it strengthens the case for multimodal fusion and may set a new best. If it does not, that suggests image features add little here and that the remaining budget should focus on the RNA encoder and aggregation.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration from llm_summary_009 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. It is the first test of image encoder choice. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6776 to 0.7062 (+0.029) and F1 from 0.6464 to 0.6671 (+0.021), making this the best result so far and about +0.056 accuracy above scVI RNA-only (llm_summary_006: 0.6501 / 0.6275). This is initial single-run evidence that ViT-L image features outperform resnet50 under weighted fusion in this setting and that stronger image features may enlarge the multimodal gain over RNA alone. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, so the +0.029 step may partly reflect noise. No image-only ViT-L run exists, so how much signal ViT-L carries alone is unmeasured. The learned modality weights were not reported. It is also untested whether ViT-L helps under concat fusion, with other RNA encoders or aggregators, or relative to other image encoders.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence on modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-complexity baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 against which every added design choice can be measured: learned or foundation RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image modality, and fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, starting from a clean baseline lets each later experiment change a single factor, such as config_002 (aggregation), config_004 (encoder) or config_016 (adding images). Without this reference, gains from more complex models could not be attributed to any specific design decision.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 was the first run in the search and established a baseline. It used an RNA-only, single-profile configuration with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (primary metric), and the validation F1 of 0.464 is broadly consistent with it. No other experiments have been completed, so this is an initial reference point only. It says nothing yet about whether learned or foundation RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image modalities, or fusion would help or hurt. Those effects can be judged only through later runs that change one factor at a time from this baseline. Run-to-run variability is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one completed run, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline. It reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. None of the other design factors has been tested, and run-to-run noise is unknown. 2) Test: config_002 changes a single factor from the baseline. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Encoder and modality stay fixed, so any change can be attributed to using multiple profiles rather than to a more complex aggregator. 3) Why now: profile setting affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, so learning its effect early helps prune many configurations. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity way to test it. This sets up later one-factor comparisons: transformer versus avgpool aggregation, alternative RNA encoders, and the image or multimodal settings.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested whether moving from single-profile to multiprofile input helps when the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) encoder is held fixed. It used the simplest aggregation (avgpool), with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose to 0.591 from the 0.485 single-profile baseline (about +0.106), and validation F1 rose in step to 0.573 from 0.464 (about +0.109). This is an initial signal that multiprofile input with avgpool may help in the RNA-only PCA setting, since this comparison changes only the profile setting and its required aggregation step. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the size and reliability of the gain are unconfirmed. It is also unclear whether the effect holds for other RNA encoders, image or multimodal settings, or stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile, with the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) encoder held fixed, raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 and F1 from 0.464 to 0.573. This is an early sign that multiprofile input helps. However, only the simplest aggregator (avgpool) has been tried, and each configuration has a single run. 2) What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 the same and changes only avgpool to a transformer. It therefore isolates the effect of the aggregation method, showing whether a learned aggregator can draw more from multiprofile input or whether avgpool is enough. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it builds directly on the most promising direction found so far, and changing one factor keeps the result easy to interpret. Knowing which aggregator works better also matters for the many later multiprofile and multimodal configurations that depend on this choice. Encoder and image-modality comparisons remain important, but they can then be run with the better-supported aggregator.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested whether a learned transformer aggregator improves on avgpool for multiprofile input. It kept the llm_summary_002 setup fixed (RNA-only, PCA n=2000 encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregation method. Validation accuracy (primary metric) was 0.519, about 0.072 below avgpool's 0.591 but still above the 0.485 single-profile baseline, and validation F1 followed the same pattern (0.480 vs 0.573 and 0.464). This is an initial signal that, in this RNA-only PCA multiprofile setting, the transformer aggregator underperformed avgpool, so avgpool is currently the better-supported choice. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, transformer training choices may not have been tuned, and it is unclear whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image modalities, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: All three runs are RNA-only with PCA n2000, one run each. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best so far (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It beat single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). The imaging modality and fusion are completely untested, and this is the largest gap in our knowledge. 2) Test: This keeps the best setup fixed (PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concat. It directly asks whether adding imaging improves on the best RNA-only model. Adding a modality necessarily brings in an image encoder and a fusion step, so this is the minimal change for that question. 3) Why now: Whether multimodal input helps is likely a bigger design decision than which RNA encoder to use. A gain would point the search toward multimodal configurations. No gain or a loss would justify focusing the budget on RNA encoders such as scVI (config_005) or scGPT (config_008). One caveat: without an image-only run, a weak result could reflect a poor image encoder rather than a fusion failure. An image-only baseline such as config_011 may be needed later to tell these apart.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested whether adding imaging helps. It kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy (primary metric) reached 0.619, about +0.028 over the 0.591 RNA-only multiprofile result and the best so far. Validation F1 rose more clearly, to 0.610 from 0.573 (about +0.038). This is an initial signal that this multimodal configuration modestly improves on RNA-only, but the change adds both an image encoder and a fusion step, so the gain cannot be attributed to the image encoder or to concat fusion separately. Every configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the small accuracy gain may not be reliable. There is also no image-only baseline (e.g., config_011) to show how much the ResNet50 branch contributes on its own. It is unclear whether other fusion methods, image encoders, or RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) would change this ranking.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: multiprofile with avgpool clearly beat single-profile in the RNA-only PCA setting (0.591 vs 0.485 accuracy). Avgpool also beat the transformer aggregator (0.591 vs 0.519). Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion gave the best result so far (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1), but the gain over RNA-only was small. That change also added both an image encoder and a fusion step, and there is no image-only reference, so it is unclear how much signal imaging carries on its own. 2) Config_011 (image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool) matches config_018 except that the RNA branch and fusion are removed. Together with config_002, it isolates each modality's standalone contribution under the same profile and aggregation setting. It will show whether images alone are weak, comparable to RNA or stronger. That tells us whether the multimodal gain reflects complementary information or mostly comes from the image branch. 3) This is the best use of the budget because it settles a basic attribution question about the image modality before spending runs on fusion variants (weighted), image encoder swaps (ViT-L) or more multimodal combinations. It reuses the best-supported profile and aggregation settings and changes only the modality.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 set up an image-only reference. It used a multiprofile ResNet50 image encoder with avgpool aggregation and no RNA branch or fusion, so it matches the multimodal llm_summary_004 setup except that the RNA branch and concat fusion are removed. It is also the image counterpart of the RNA-only llm_summary_002 under the same profile and aggregation settings. Validation accuracy (primary metric) was 0.328 and validation F1 was 0.288, far below RNA-only multiprofile (0.591/0.573) and multimodal concat (0.619/0.610), and also below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.485). This is an initial signal that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features carry much weaker standalone signal than PCA RNA features, and that the multimodal result depends mainly on the RNA branch, with any image contribution being modest at best. Whether images add complementary information or the small multimodal gain reflects run-to-run noise or the fusion step itself remains unresolved. Uncertainties include single runs with unknown variance, possible lack of tuning for the image branch, and whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), other aggregators, or other fusion schemes would change the image-only or multimodal picture.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the signal so far. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, versus 0.328 for image-only. Multimodal concat added only about +0.028 accuracy, which may be within run-to-run noise. Multiprofile with avgpool was the best-supported profile and aggregation setting. Yet every result so far uses the PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, so the effect of RNA representation is completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_005 swaps PCA for scVI (n=200) and keeps everything else as in config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It therefore isolates the effect of the RNA encoder on the dominant modality. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: because RNA drives performance, the RNA encoder choice is likely the highest-impact open question. The result will directly guide which RNA encoder to use in later multimodal and fusion experiments. Tuning fusion or image encoders now would refine a small secondary contribution while leaving this larger uncertainty unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested the RNA encoder choice. It swapped PCA (n=2000) for scVI (n=200) and otherwise kept the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup of llm_summary_002, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose to 0.650 from 0.591 (about +0.059), and validation F1 rose in step to 0.628 from 0.573 (about +0.055). This is the best result so far, above even the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat run (0.619 accuracy), though that comparison is not controlled. This is an initial signal that scVI is the stronger RNA representation in this setting, but the swap changes both the encoder method and the dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so their effects cannot be separated. Each configuration also has a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, and it remains untested whether the gain carries over to multimodal or fusion settings, holds against other aggregators, or would be matched by other encoders such as scGPT or a different scVI latent size.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder has had the largest controlled effect so far. Swapping PCA for scVI in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (F1 0.573 to 0.628), the best result yet. Adding ResNet50 images to PCA gave a smaller, unattributed gain (+0.028), and images alone were weak (0.328). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, appears in a third of the search space but is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best-supported setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This gives a clean three-way encoder comparison and shows whether a foundation-model representation beats scVI. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Encoder choice appears to be the most important lever, and this run decides whether the many scGPT configurations deserve further budget. It also determines which encoder to carry forward into fusion tests (for example config_030 vs config_042). Running it now avoids committing early to scVI-based multimodal runs whose expected image gain is modest.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 completed a controlled three-way RNA encoder comparison. It kept the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setup of llm_summary_002 and llm_summary_006 (no image encoder or fusion) and swapped in the scGPT foundation-model encoder. Validation accuracy (primary metric) was 0.530, below both scVI (0.650) and PCA n=2000 (0.591), and validation F1 followed the same order (0.515 vs 0.628 and 0.573). This is an initial signal that, in this setting, scGPT is the weakest of the three RNA representations and scVI remains the best-supported encoder to carry into fusion tests. However, each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance, and scGPT's embedding setup (e.g., whether it was fine-tuned or frozen, preprocessing, gene-vocabulary overlap) may not have been optimized. It also remains untested whether scGPT would rank differently with other aggregators, with image fusion, or in single-profile settings, so the many untested scGPT configurations look lower priority but are not ruled out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.650 accuracy, RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool), ahead of PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion to the PCA setup gave a modest gain (0.591 to 0.619 accuracy, 0.573 to 0.610 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.328), so it is unclear whether images add complementary signal or whether that gain was noise. 2) This experiment adds the same ResNet50 branch and concat fusion to the best scVI setup, with profile setting and aggregation unchanged. It differs from config_005 only in the added image branch and from config_018 only in the RNA encoder. That gives two controlled comparisons: whether the image gain persists, shrinks or reverses when the RNA representation is stronger, and whether scVI's advantage carries into the multimodal setting. 3) It is the logical extension of the best-supported choices (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and has a good chance of a new best result. It also tests a key design question, whether multimodal fusion is worth its cost with a strong RNA encoder, before spending budget on secondary choices such as weighted fusion or ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 added the ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (scVI n=200, multiprofile, avgpool), which gives two controlled comparisons: against llm_summary_006, where only the image branch and fusion were added, and against llm_summary_004, where only the RNA encoder was swapped from PCA n=2000. Validation accuracy (primary metric) was 0.632 with F1 0.607, about 0.019 accuracy and 0.021 F1 below scVI RNA-only (0.650/0.628), so the small image gain seen with PCA (+0.028 accuracy) did not carry over and slightly reversed with the stronger RNA encoder. Against the PCA multimodal run (0.619/0.610), scVI kept only a small accuracy edge (+0.013) and F1 was essentially tied (-0.004), so scVI's RNA-only advantage (+0.059) mostly disappeared under concat fusion. This is an initial signal that ResNet50 concat fusion does not help, and may slightly hurt, when the RNA representation is strong, and scVI RNA-only remains the best-supported configuration; however, all differences are small single-run gaps with unknown run-to-run variance, the image-plus-fusion addition cannot be separated into image-encoder and concat-fusion effects, and it remains untested whether weighted or other fusion schemes, a stronger image encoder such as ViT-L, or tuning of the fusion head would let images add complementary signal.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_005) is the best run so far, at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered this, to 0.632 and 0.607. ResNet50 image-only was weak, at 0.328. So concat may let a weak image branch dilute strong RNA features, but it is unclear whether the problem is the image signal or the fusion scheme. 2. What this tests: config_031 changes only concat to weighted fusion and keeps scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. A weighted scheme can learn to down-weight the weaker modality. If it matches or beats scVI RNA-only, that points to fusion design as the bottleneck and suggests images can still add complementary signal. If it also underperforms, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 adds little here, and the remaining budget can go to a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or to RNA-side refinements. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a clean single-factor comparison on the most important open question, whether multimodality helps at all with the best RNA encoder. It also has a realistic chance of becoming the new best, so it balances exploration and exploitation. All gaps so far are small single-run differences with unknown variance, so the result should be read as an initial signal rather than a firm ranking.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a single-factor test against llm_summary_008: it kept scVI n=200, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed and changed only concat fusion to weighted fusion. It reached 0.678 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.646 F1, the best result so far. That is about +0.046 accuracy and +0.040 F1 over concat (0.632/0.607), and about +0.028 accuracy and +0.019 F1 over scVI RNA-only (llm_summary_006, 0.650/0.628). This is an initial signal that the fusion scheme, not just the image signal, limited the earlier multimodal run, and that with weighted fusion the multimodal scVI+ResNet50 setup can exceed RNA-only despite the weak image-only result (0.328 accuracy). The comparison with concat isolates fusion type, but each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the gains are small and unconfirmed. Several questions remain untested: whether the learned weights actually down-weight the image branch, whether the gain over RNA-only reflects complementary image information or other properties of the weighted fusion head, and whether weighted fusion helps with PCA RNA, a stronger image encoder such as ViT-L, or other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: weighted fusion gives the best result so far (config_031: 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). It beats concat by about 0.046 accuracy and scVI RNA-only by about 0.028. Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.328), so the image branch is the likely bottleneck. The image encoder is the one major design choice still untested, since every image run so far used ResNet50. 2) Test: config_037 keeps scVI n=200, multiprofile, avgpool and weighted fusion fixed and changes only ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This shows whether a stronger image representation adds complementary signal under weighted fusion. A gain would support images being useful when well represented and fused. No gain or a drop would suggest the image contribution is limited and would focus effort on RNA, fusion or aggregation. 3) Why now: it is a controlled single-factor extension of the best configuration. It explores a new design axis and also has a good chance of beating the current best. That is more informative than testing the transformer aggregator, which has already underperformed avgpool, or scGPT variants, whose encoder ranked weakest.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was a single-factor test against llm_summary_009. It kept scVI n=200 RNA, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion fixed, and swapped only the ResNet50 image encoder for ImageNet ViT-L. It reached 0.706 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.667 F1, the best result so far: about +0.029 accuracy and +0.021 F1 over the ResNet50 weighted-fusion run (0.678/0.646), and about +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1 over scVI RNA-only (0.650/0.628). This is an initial signal that a stronger image representation adds useful signal under weighted fusion, which suggests the image branch was a bottleneck rather than imaging being uninformative. However, each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the gain is small and unconfirmed. There is also no ViT-L image-only baseline, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects stronger standalone image features or complementary signal (or properties such as embedding size), and it remains untested whether ViT-L helps under concat fusion, with PCA RNA, or with other aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration and serves as a baseline. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only), and fusion (multimodal). 3) Running the simplest model first avoids assuming that complexity helps and gives a clean reference for judging later gains. It also uses one experiment without confounding several design choices at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components). It used no image encoder, no aggregation and no fusion, and was chosen as the simplest reference configuration. It reached validation accuracy 0.4849 (supporting F1 0.4639). This is only an initial reference point, because there are no comparison runs and the number of classes and chance level are not given, so it is unclear how good this result is. It is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multi-profile settings with aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better. Later experiments should change one factor at a time against this baseline so that any gains can be attributed.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only one baseline exists (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, val acc 0.485, F1 0.464), so no design factor has been tested yet. 2) This run changes one thing: it switches from single-profile to multi-profile input, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). The RNA encoder and modality stay the same, so any change in accuracy or F1 can be credited to using multiple profiles. 3) Profile setting splits the remaining search space roughly in half and applies to the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal branches alike. Settling it early, with the cheapest aggregator, tells us whether multi-profile variants (and later transformer aggregation) are worth budget. Encoder and modality comparisons (e.g., scVI single-profile, image-only) are natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only, multi-profile model with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder and average-pooling aggregation, and no image encoder or fusion. It differs from baseline llm_summary_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) in using multi-profile input, which also requires adding avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (about +0.106), and supporting F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (about +0.109). This is an initial observation that multi-profile input with avgpool may help in the RNA-only PCA setting, but the evidence is limited: it rests on one run per configuration with no seeds or variance estimates, the effect of multiple profiles cannot be separated from the choice of aggregator, and it is unknown whether the gain holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only or multimodal models, or other aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multi-profile input with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose by a similar amount. Because multi-profile input requires an aggregator, this gain mixes two effects: having multiple profiles, and the choice of avgpool. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best run (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multi-profile) and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether a learned aggregator adds value over simple pooling. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a one-factor extension of the strongest result so far, so it has good immediate upside. Aggregation also appears in many later multi-profile, image-only and multimodal configurations, so this answer is reusable across much of the remaining search.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the current best configuration (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool (llm_summary_002) to a transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (about -0.072), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (about -0.093). This one-factor comparison suggests that in this setting the transformer aggregator did not improve on simple average pooling and may have underperformed it, although it stayed slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.4849 accuracy, 0.4639 F1). The result is uncertain because each configuration has only one run with no seeds or variance estimates, the transformer's hyperparameters and training adequacy (for example, whether it underfit or overfit) are unknown, and it is unclear whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models or multimodal models.

selection_reason: Evidence: all three runs are RNA-only with PCA-2000. Multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat single-profile (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519), but these are single runs with no seed variance. The image modality is completely untested, yet most remaining configurations (image-only and all multimodal) depend on it. This experiment tests whether ResNet50 image features carry useful signal on their own. It keeps the best-performing profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile + avgpool) fixed, so the result can be compared directly with config_002 as an image-versus-RNA modality comparison. It is the best use of budget because it resolves the largest uncertainty in the search space: a strong result would justify exploring fusion and the ViT-L encoder, while a weak result would let us deprioritize many image-dependent configurations. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) remains a useful next step but affects a smaller part of the decision.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was the first test of the image modality. It used an image-only, multi-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and avgpool aggregation, no RNA encoder and no fusion, so it differs from llm_summary_002 (RNA-only PCA-2000, multi-profile, avgpool) only in the input modality and encoder. Validation accuracy was 0.3275 (supporting F1 0.2884), far below llm_summary_002 (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1; about -0.263 and -0.284) and below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4849 accuracy). This initial observation suggests that ResNet50 image features alone carry weaker signal than PCA-2000 RNA features in this setting. It is uncertain because each configuration has one run with no seed variance, the number of classes and chance level are unknown (so it is unclear whether 0.33 is meaningfully above chance), ResNet50 training details such as pretraining and freezing are unknown, and it is untested whether ViT-L would do better or whether image features still add complementary value when fused with RNA.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within RNA-only PCA-2000 models, multiprofile input with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) clearly beat the single-profile baseline (0.485) and the transformer aggregator (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool was much weaker (0.328 accuracy). Fusion is still completely untested, so we do not know whether image features add complementary signal or only add noise. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the current best setup (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Both of its unimodal parts have already been measured, so the result directly isolates whether adding the image modality helps or hurts relative to config_002. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Whether to go multimodal is one of the largest design choices and a large part of the remaining search space. It determines whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal configurations or to RNA-only alternatives such as the scVI and scGPT encoders. Concat is the simplest fusion option, so it is the cleanest first test before trying weighted fusion or the ViT-L image encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was the first multimodal test. It kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multi-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy was 0.6186 (supporting F1 0.6103), modestly above llm_summary_002 (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1; about +0.028 and +0.038) and well above the image-only ResNet50 run (0.3275). This initial one-factor comparison suggests that image features may add some complementary signal to RNA rather than only adding noise, even though images alone were weak. The gain is small and rests on single runs with no seeds or variance estimates, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. It is also unknown whether the benefit would hold or grow with other fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion), a stronger image encoder (ViT-L), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or different training details such as encoder freezing or pretraining.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant signal. RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool reached 0.591, image-only ResNet50 reached 0.328, and fusion added only a small +0.028 (best 0.619, config_018). Multiprofile with avgpool beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Every RNA run so far used PCA-2000, so the choice of RNA representation is the largest untested design factor, and it acts on the modality that drives performance. 2) What this tests: config_008 keeps the best RNA-only setup from config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. That gives a clean one-factor comparison of RNA representation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: tweaking fusion (weighted) or the image encoder (ViT-L) works on a secondary signal, so expected gains are small and could fall within run-to-run noise. A better RNA encoder could shift the whole search, including which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal runs. scGPT is the encoder most different from PCA, so the comparison is the most informative whichever way it turns out.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 (multi-profile, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT. It was the first test of a non-PCA RNA representation. Validation accuracy was 0.5305 (supporting F1 0.5152), below the PCA-2000 counterpart (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1; about -0.060 and -0.057) but above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This one-factor comparison suggests that scGPT embeddings did not beat PCA-2000 in this setting and may have underperformed it, so PCA-2000 remains the strongest RNA encoder observed so far. The result is uncertain for several reasons: each configuration has a single run with no seed variance, scGPT usage details (frozen versus fine-tuned, pretraining match, gene vocabulary overlap) are unknown, and it is untested whether scVI would do better or whether the PCA-versus-scGPT ranking holds in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Its small gain over RNA-only (+0.028) suggests images add some complementary signal. However, ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.3275), so the image representation may be limiting the benefit. The image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) is completely untested. The RNA encoder, aggregation and profile setting already have at least one comparison each. 2) Test: config_024 keeps config_018 fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain, which also helps tell whether the +0.028 fusion benefit is real or noise. 3) Why this experiment: it is a clean one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it can plausibly improve accuracy while resolving a key untested design choice. Testing weighted fusion or scVI is also worthwhile, but the image encoder is the most likely bottleneck on the multimodal path.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_005 fixed (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This was the first test of ViT-L. Validation accuracy was 0.6287, slightly above llm_summary_005 (0.6186; about +0.010) and making it the best result so far, but supporting F1 fell (0.5993 vs 0.6103; about -0.011), and both runs remain above the RNA-only PCA-2000 counterpart llm_summary_002 (0.5907 accuracy, 0.5727 F1). This one-factor comparison is an initial observation that ViT-L may give a marginal accuracy gain in fusion, but the change is small, the two metrics disagree, and each configuration has a single run with no seed variance, so the difference may be within noise and does not clearly show that a stronger image encoder increases the multimodal benefit. It is still untested whether ViT-L beats ResNet50 in an image-only setting, whether the result depends on encoder details such as freezing or fine-tuning, and whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion) or RNA encoders (scVI) would change the ranking.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287 accuracy. Several design choices have each been compared once: multiprofile beat singleprofile, avgpool beat transformer, PCA beat scGPT, and adding image features to RNA helped. Fusion is the one design dimension never varied, since every multimodal run used concat. The ResNet50 vs ViT-L difference is small and the two metrics disagree on it. 2. What this tests: Changing only concat to weighted fusion on the current best setup isolates the effect of the fusion method. Weighted fusion may also suit this data, because image features were weak on their own and weighting could let the model lean on RNA while still using the complementary image signal. 3. Why this is the best next run: It explores an entirely untested design axis and also exploits the strongest configuration. Whichever way it turns out, it tells us whether fusion matters before spending budget on secondary questions such as scVI or image-only ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration from llm_summary_007 fixed (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. This was the first time fusion was varied. Validation accuracy was 0.6352, slightly above llm_summary_007 (0.6287; about +0.007) and the best result so far, and supporting F1 rose more clearly (0.6183 vs 0.5993; about +0.019), also exceeding the previous best F1 from llm_summary_005 (ResNet50 + concat, 0.6103). This one-factor comparison is an initial observation that weighted fusion may modestly help, or at least not hurt, in this setup, and here both metrics agree, unlike the ViT-L vs ResNet50 comparison. However, the accuracy gain is small and each configuration has a single run with no seed variance, so the difference may be within noise. It is also untested whether weighted fusion helps with ResNet50 or other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), what the learned modality weights are (for example, whether the model leans mostly on RNA), and whether other fusion schemes would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is one of the most influential choices so far. PCA-2000 beat scGPT by about 0.06 accuracy in the RNA-only multi-profile avgpool setting. RNA also dominates the multimodal models, where image features add only small gains (about +0.01 to +0.03). scVI is the only RNA encoder never tested, which is the largest remaining gap in a high-impact design dimension. The current best configuration is config_025 (PCA-2000 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.635 accuracy / 0.618 F1). 2) Test: config_037 keeps config_025 fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This shows whether a compact probabilistic RNA representation can match or beat PCA when fused with image features. It also shows whether the PCA-over-learned-embedding pattern seen with scGPT extends to scVI. 3) Budget value: as a one-factor change from the best configuration, it both explores the untested encoder and exploits the strongest known setup. A win would directly improve the best result, and a loss would strengthen the case that PCA-2000 is the right RNA encoder. Either way it settles an important design choice in one run. A limitation: the image branch could partly mask RNA encoder differences, so an RNA-only scVI run (config_005) is a natural follow-up if the result is ambiguous.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the previous best configuration from llm_summary_008 fixed (multimodal, multi-profile, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, which was the first test of scVI. Validation accuracy was 0.7062 (supporting F1 0.6671), the best result so far by a clear margin over llm_summary_008 (0.6352 accuracy, 0.6183 F1; about +0.071 and +0.049). Both metrics agree, and the gain is much larger than earlier image-encoder and fusion changes (about +0.01). This one-factor comparison suggests that scVI-200 may be a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this fused setup, which contrasts with the earlier RNA-only finding that scGPT underperformed PCA (llm_summary_006), so the PCA-over-learned-embedding pattern does not appear to extend to scVI. It remains uncertain because each configuration has a single run with no seed variance, scVI training details are unknown, and the gain may partly reflect interaction with ViT-L or weighted fusion. An RNA-only scVI multi-profile avgpool run would show whether scVI's advantage holds without the image branch, and it is also untested with concat fusion, ResNet50, or a transformer aggregator.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 gave by far the largest single-factor gain so far (+0.071 accuracy, +0.049 F1), reaching 0.706 accuracy in the multimodal ViT-L weighted-fusion setup. Earlier image-encoder and fusion changes moved accuracy by only about 0.01. It is still unclear whether scVI is a better RNA representation on its own or whether its gain depends on interaction with ViT-L and weighted fusion. In RNA-only runs, scGPT underperformed PCA, so learned embeddings are not uniformly better. 2. What this tests: config_005 runs RNA-only scVI-200 with multi-profile input and avgpool. It differs in one factor from config_002 (PCA RNA-only, 0.591) and config_008 (scGPT RNA-only, 0.530), giving a clean encoder comparison without images. It also differs from config_037 only by removing the image branch, which measures how much ViT-L contributes on top of scVI. With PCA, adding images was worth about +0.03 to +0.04. 3. Why this is the best next run: The RNA encoder now looks like the most influential design choice, so confirming its effect is the most valuable uncertainty to resolve. The result will guide later budget use: whether to keep investing in image and fusion variants, or to focus on RNA representation and aggregation with scVI.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, multi-profile model with a scVI-200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It differs only in the RNA encoder from llm_summary_002 (PCA-2000, 0.5907 accuracy) and llm_summary_006 (scGPT, 0.5305 accuracy). It differs from llm_summary_009 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, weighted fusion, 0.7062 accuracy) only by removing the image branch and its fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.6501 (supporting F1 0.6275), about +0.060 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over PCA-2000 and about +0.120 and +0.112 over scGPT. It also exceeds every PCA-based multimodal run, including llm_summary_008 at 0.6352. These clean one-factor comparisons suggest that scVI-200 may be a stronger RNA representation on its own, not only through interaction with ViT-L or weighted fusion. Removing ViT-L with weighted fusion cost about -0.056 accuracy and -0.040 F1, which suggests images still add complementary signal on top of scVI, comparable to or slightly larger than the roughly +0.03 to +0.045 image benefit seen with PCA. Uncertainty remains because each configuration has a single run with no seed variance, so small differences such as the scVI-versus-PCA image benefit may be within noise. scVI training details are also unknown, and it is untested whether scVI's advantage holds with a transformer aggregator, single-profile input, other scVI latent sizes, or other image encoders and fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 is RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (2000-component) encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a simple, interpretable reference point. Each later experiment can then change one factor against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile with avgpool, an image-only model, or a multimodal fusion model. 3) Under a limited budget, starting with the simplest configuration makes later comparisons attributable to single design changes. It also tests whether added complexity is needed at all, without assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will win.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration as a reference point: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.464 (supporting). F1 is slightly below accuracy, which may suggest somewhat uneven performance across classes. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only a baseline: it says nothing yet about the effect of the RNA encoder, the profile setting, aggregation, the image modality, or multimodal fusion. It is also unknown how close this score is to chance or to the best achievable performance, and seed-to-seed variance has not been measured. Future experiments should change one factor at a time against this baseline, such as using a scVI or scGPT encoder, a multiprofile setting with avgpool, an image-only model, or fusion, so that any differences can be traced to that change.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only one result exists, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We do not know whether the image modality carries useful signal. That question underlies every multimodal and fusion configuration, which make up most of the remaining search space. 2) Test: config_010 is an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. It is a clean modality comparison against the baseline, since profile setting, aggregation and fusion are all held constant. 3) Why now: if images are weak, many multimodal configurations become lower priority. If images are comparable or stronger, fusion becomes a promising direction. Either outcome narrows the large multimodal space more than an RNA encoder swap such as config_004 or config_007, which tests one RNA factor without saying whether the image half of the space is worth exploring. A single run will not settle the question, but it is the cheapest way to decide where the next experiments should go.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a modality comparison against the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline from llm_summary_001 (val acc 0.485, F1 0.464). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.172, well below the RNA-only baseline, so this image-only ResNet50 configuration appears much weaker on its own; the F1 gap below accuracy may again suggest uneven performance across classes. Modality and encoder changed together, so the gap cannot be attributed to the image modality in general rather than to ResNet50 specifically, and each result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance and an unknown chance level. Images may still add complementary signal when fused with RNA, so a lower priority for image-heavy configurations is reasonable but unconfirmed; a direct RNA+image fusion test against the RNA-only baseline, or an alternative image encoder, would help resolve this.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA single-profile (config_001) is the strongest result so far (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile (config_010) is much weaker (acc 0.208). We do not yet know whether the profile setting or aggregation matters. That choice runs through most of the remaining search space, across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). The RNA modality and PCA encoder stay fixed. Any change from config_001 can therefore be attributed to using multiple profiles. 3) Why now: if multiprofile clearly helps, the search can focus on multiprofile variants and compare transformer against avgpool next. If it does not help, we avoid spending budget on many multiprofile configurations. It also builds on the best-performing branch rather than the weak image branch. RNA encoder (scVI/scGPT) and fusion tests remain good follow-ups once this factor is clearer.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It is a near one-factor comparison against the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: val acc 0.485, F1 0.464). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.573, about +0.106 accuracy and +0.109 F1 over the baseline, making it the best result so far and suggesting that a multiprofile setup with simple avgpool aggregation benefits the RNA-PCA branch. Uncertainty remains: the multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, so the gain cannot be separated between them. Each result is also a single run with unmeasured seed variance, and it is unknown whether the benefit extends to other RNA encoders (scVI/scGPT), image-only, or fused configurations. A transformer-vs-avgpool comparison under multiprofile, and multiprofile tests on other branches, are natural next steps.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591, F1 0.573). That is about +0.11 accuracy over the single-profile baseline. However, multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so the gain cannot yet be split between them. Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.208), which lowers but does not rule out the value of images. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 fixed and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This is a clean one-factor comparison. It shows whether a learned attention-based aggregator adds to the multiprofile benefit, or whether simple pooling is enough. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result and resolves an aggregation choice that affects every downstream multiprofile config, including the RNA, image and multimodal ones. It changes a single variable, so the result stays interpretable. Testing encoder alternatives or fusion is better done after the aggregation choice under multiprofile is clearer.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 was a clean one-factor comparison against the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n=2000, avgpool; val acc 0.591, F1 0.573), with avgpool swapped for transformer aggregation and everything else held fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.480, which is about 0.072 accuracy and 0.093 F1 below avgpool. In this setting, the learned attention-based aggregator therefore underperformed simple pooling, and the larger F1 drop may suggest more uneven performance across classes. The result still sits modestly above the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.485), which tentatively suggests that multiprofile input helps under either aggregator, though this is not a fully isolated test of the profile setting. Uncertainties remain: each result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance; the transformer's hyperparameters and training budget may not have been tuned, so this may reflect the specific setup rather than transformer aggregation in general; and it is unknown whether avgpool's advantage holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or fused multiprofile configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000 with avgpool (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat single-profile PCA (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), so fusion looks less promising for now. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice, because only PCA has been tried. 2) This run keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only PCA n2000 for scVI n200. That isolates the effect of the RNA representation, and the result will show whether the multiprofile/avgpool gain carries over to a learned latent encoder. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it exploits the strongest configuration while settling the main remaining uncertainty with a single-factor change. It could also produce a new best. Whichever encoder wins then gives a stronger RNA backbone for later fusion tests.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 was a clean one-factor comparison against the previous best configuration (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n=2000, avgpool; val acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It swapped only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, and kept the multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.628, about +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over PCA, which makes it the new best result. This suggests that, in this setup, the learned scVI latent representation is a stronger RNA backbone than PCA and that the multiprofile/avgpool configuration still works well with a learned encoder. Uncertainties remain: each result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, and the encoder type and dimensionality (200 vs 2000) changed together, so the gain cannot be attributed to scVI specifically rather than to latent size. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds under single-profile or transformer aggregation, how it compares with other encoders such as scGPT, and whether this stronger RNA branch benefits from image fusion given the weak image-only ResNet50 result (acc 0.208).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is scVI n200 with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation (config_005: acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Multiprofile with avgpool and the scVI encoder have each shown gains in near one-factor comparisons, although each result is a single run. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (acc 0.208). However, no multimodal configuration has been tested, so we do not know whether image features add complementary signal to a strong RNA branch. This is the largest untested design axis. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps the best setup fixed (scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 relative to config_005 can therefore be attributed mainly to adding the image modality. ResNet50 is the only image encoder already characterized, and concat is the simplest fusion, which avoids adding another untested factor. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a one-factor test of whether multimodality helps. If accuracy improves, it may set a new best and justify exploring weighted fusion and ViT-L image encoders. If accuracy falls or stays flat, it justifies putting less budget into the many multimodal configurations and more into RNA-encoder comparisons such as scGPT (config_008).
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 was a one-factor test of multimodality. It kept the best RNA-only configuration (llm_summary_005: scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool; val acc 0.650, F1 0.628) fixed and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.632 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.607, about 0.019 accuracy and 0.021 F1 below the RNA-only counterpart, so in this setup adding ResNet50 image features via concat did not help and may have slightly hurt. This is consistent with the weak image-only ResNet50 result (acc 0.208) and tentatively supports giving RNA-encoder comparisons (e.g., scGPT) priority over broad multimodal exploration. Uncertainties remain: the drop is small, and each result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, so the gap may be within noise. The result reflects only one image encoder and the simplest fusion, so it does not rule out benefits from a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or from weighted or learned fusion, which might keep a weak image branch from diluting the RNA signal.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool. Within that setting, scVI n200 (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) beat PCA n2000 (0.591). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation with PCA (0.591 vs 0.519). Adding ResNet50 images via concat fusion slightly lowered the scVI result (0.632), and image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208). The RNA encoder is the largest lever measured so far, but scGPT, the third encoder option, is still untested. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT and keeps the best known setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). It is a clean one-factor comparison against config_005 and config_002, and it will show whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats scVI as the RNA backbone. 3) It covers both exploitation and exploration. It is a plausible path to a new best, and it settles the remaining encoder question before more budget goes to multimodal, image-encoder (ViT-L), or fusion variants. Whichever RNA encoder wins should anchor those later fusion tests.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 was a clean one-factor RNA-encoder comparison: it swapped scVI n200 (llm_summary_005: val acc 0.650, F1 0.628) and PCA n2000 (llm_summary_003: acc 0.591, F1 0.573) for scGPT embeddings, holding the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.530 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.515, about 0.120 accuracy below scVI and 0.061 below PCA, so in this setup the pretrained foundation-model embedding was the weakest of the three RNA encoders tested. This tentatively makes scVI n200 the RNA backbone to anchor future multimodal, image-encoder (e.g., ViT-L), or fusion tests. Uncertainties remain: each result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, and the scGPT embedding dimension, whether it was frozen or fine-tuned, and how well its preprocessing and gene vocabulary matched this data are unknown, so this may reflect the specific setup rather than scGPT in general, and the result is untested under single-profile or other aggregation and fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI n200 with multiprofile and avgpool is the best result so far (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). Adding ResNet50 through concat fusion (config_030) gave slightly lower scores (acc 0.632, F1 0.607). That drop is small and comes from a single run, so it may be noise. It is also unclear whether images add nothing or whether naive concat lets the weak image branch (image-only acc 0.208) dilute the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_031 changes only one factor from config_030, swapping concat for weighted fusion with the same scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool setup. This isolates the effect of the fusion method. If weighted fusion matches or beats the RNA-only best, the image branch can contribute once it is down-weighted. If it does not, the case for prioritizing RNA-only refinements gets stronger. 3) Why now: it is a clean single-factor comparison against an existing result, and it settles an open design choice (fusion) that affects every remaining multimodal configuration. It also has a reasonable chance of producing the new best accuracy. Testing a ViT-L image encoder makes sense after this, once we know whether the fusion method can use image features.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 was a clean one-factor fusion comparison against llm_summary_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; val acc 0.632, F1 0.607): it swapped concat for weighted fusion and held everything else fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.646. That is about +0.046 accuracy and +0.040 F1 over concat, and about +0.028 accuracy and +0.019 F1 over the RNA-only scVI best (llm_summary_005: acc 0.650, F1 0.628), making it the new best result. This suggests that in this setup weighted fusion handles the ResNet50 branch better than concat, and it tentatively indicates that images can add complementary signal despite weak image-only performance (acc 0.208). Uncertainties remain: every result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, so the modest margin over RNA-only may be within noise. The learned fusion weights were not reported, so it is unknown whether the gain comes from down-weighting the image branch or from another effect of the fusion mechanism. It is also untested whether the gain holds with a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or with other RNA encoders and aggregation settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). It beat both concat fusion (0.632) and RNA-only scVI (0.650), even though ResNet50 alone was weak (0.208). The key open question is whether the image branch is limited by its encoder. ImageNet ViT-L has not been tested anywhere. 2. Test: config_037 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. This isolates the effect of the image encoder under the strongest RNA backbone, profile setting, aggregation and fusion. If ViT-L supplies more complementary signal, accuracy and F1 should rise above 0.678/0.646. If it does not, the image modality's contribution is probably capped regardless of encoder. 3. Why now: it is both exploitation, since it is the most likely route to a new best, and a clean one-factor answer to a major untested design choice. That is more budget-efficient than an image-only ViT-L run, which would not directly show complementarity in fusion, or than revisiting aggregation or scGPT variants, which already look weaker.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 was a clean one-factor image-encoder comparison against the previous best (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; val acc 0.678, F1 0.646). It swapped ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L and held everything else fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.667, about +0.029 accuracy and +0.021 F1 over ResNet50 and about +0.056 accuracy over the RNA-only scVI model (llm_summary_005: acc 0.650), which makes it the new best result. This suggests that, in this setup, the image branch was partly limited by its encoder and that ViT-L supplies more complementary signal under weighted fusion. Uncertainties remain: every result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, so the modest margin may be within noise. ViT-L image-only performance was not measured, and the learned fusion weights were not reported, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects stronger standalone image features or better complementarity. It is also untested whether ViT-L helps under concat fusion, with other RNA encoders, or with other aggregation settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the current best is config_037 (scVI n200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Fusion is one of the largest open design questions. With ResNet50, weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.046 accuracy, and concat even fell below RNA-only. That suggests concat lets a weak image branch dilute the RNA signal. It is unknown whether weighted fusion is still needed once the image branch is stronger (ViT-L), or whether the earlier gap was specific to ResNet50. 2) This experiment swaps only weighted fusion for concat in the best configuration. If concat with ViT-L roughly matches weighted, the fusion choice matters mainly for weak image encoders. If concat stays clearly worse, weighted fusion is a robust design choice for the rest of the search. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest result and tests the fusion × image-encoder interaction. It is more informative than retesting transformer aggregation, which already underperformed avgpool once, or the weaker scGPT and PCA branches. It also stays close to the high-performing region, so the result could still be competitive.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 was a clean one-factor fusion comparison against the previous best, llm_summary_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200 + ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; val acc 0.706, F1 0.667), swapping weighted fusion for concat with everything else held fixed. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.687, about +0.009 accuracy and +0.020 F1 over weighted fusion, which makes it nominally the new best result. This contrasts with the ResNet50 pair, where concat trailed weighted by about 0.046 accuracy and fell below RNA-only (llm_summary_006 vs 008), so the weighted-fusion advantage may depend on a weak image encoder rather than being robust. Uncertainties remain: every result is a single run with unmeasured seed variance, so the small accuracy margin may be within noise and the two fusion methods should be treated as roughly comparable with ViT-L. Learned fusion weights and ViT-L image-only performance are unreported, so the mechanism is unclear, and it is untested whether this fusion × encoder pattern holds with other RNA encoders or aggregation settings.

selection_reason: 1) There is no evidence yet. Nothing is known about how modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect accuracy. 2) The RNA-only, single-profile PCA (pca_n2000) model is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline that every later comparison can be measured against: scVI or scGPT versus PCA, multiprofile versus single-profile, image versus RNA, and multimodal versus unimodal. 3) Starting with a cheap, low-variance anchor is the best first use of the budget. It avoids assuming that complexity helps, and it lets each later experiment change one design choice relative to a known reference, so we can tell which choices actually matter.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a low-cost reference point for later one-change comparisons. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. The two numbers are close, which suggests performance is not heavily concentrated in a few classes, though this cannot be confirmed without per-class results. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial baseline. It is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings, image modalities, or multimodal fusion would improve accuracy. Run-to-run variance and the expected chance-level accuracy for this task are also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001: accuracy 0.4849, F1 0.4639). We have no information yet about any other design axis. 2) Test: config_002 changes one thing, switching to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). RNA-only and the pca_n2000 encoder stay fixed, so any gain or loss can be attributed to the profile setting rather than to the encoder or modality. 3) Why now: the profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, since most untested configurations are multiprofile. Learning early whether pooling multiple profiles helps tells us whether to prioritize multiprofile variants, including transformer aggregation and multimodal ones. Avgpool is a cheap, low-variance first test before trying the more complex transformer aggregation. Encoder and image-modality comparisons remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed one design axis from the llm_summary_001 baseline: it switched the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), while keeping the RNA-only modality and pca_n2000 encoder fixed. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (+0.106), and validation F1 rose in parallel from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (+0.109). This suggests that multiprofile input with mean pooling helps under this RNA-only PCA setup, which supports prioritizing multiprofile variants, though the gain reflects the multiprofile setting and avgpool together rather than either one alone. Each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size and reliability of the gain are uncertain, and it remains untested whether transformer aggregation, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image modalities, or fusion would change or add to this effect.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one run per configuration. RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) beat singleprofile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1). That favors multiprofile, but nothing is known about the image modality, which appears in 42 of the 49 remaining configurations, all image-only or multimodal. 2) Test: config_011 keeps the best known setup fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, no fusion) and changes only the modality, from RNA (pca_n2000) to image (resnet50). It measures how much signal images carry on their own. It also checks whether the multiprofile setup works for images too, not just RNA. 3) Why now: knowing whether images are weak, comparable or stronger than RNA decides whether the large multimodal space is worth pursuing. It also tells us whether the budget should go to RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) or aggregation comparisons instead. That makes it a higher-value reduction of uncertainty than a smaller within-RNA change, such as transformer aggregation in config_003.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the llm_summary_002 setup fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, no fusion) and switched from RNA-only with pca_n2000 to image-only with a resnet50 image encoder, to measure how much signal images carry on their own. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 (F1 0.2884). That is well below the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1) and also below the RNA-only singleprofile baseline (0.4849 acc), so in this setup the resnet50 image features appear considerably weaker than PCA RNA features. Because the modality and the encoder changed together, this gap cannot be attributed to the image modality in general rather than to this resnet50/avgpool pipeline. The F1-accuracy gap (~0.039) is slightly wider than in the RNA runs, which may hint at less even per-class performance, but this is unconfirmed without per-class results. Several things remain uncertain: whether images add complementary signal under multimodal fusion despite their weak standalone performance, whether other image encoders or transformer aggregation would narrow the gap, and whether multiprofile helps images as it did RNA (no singleprofile image run exists). With a single run per configuration and unknown chance level, the reliability of these differences is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile pca_n2000 with avgpool (config_002: acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Multiprofile gave a sizable gain over singleprofile (0.485). Image-only resnet50 with the same multiprofile/avgpool setup was much weaker (0.328 acc). The central open question is whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA, despite their weak standalone performance. 2) config_018 keeps the multiprofile, avgpool, pca_n2000 and resnet50 settings from configs 002 and 011 and adds only concat fusion. It is therefore a clean one-change comparison against both unimodal runs. It will show whether multimodal fusion beats the RNA-only result, matches it, or degrades it because of noisy image features. Accuracy is the main measure, with F1 as support. 3) The answer shapes the rest of the search. If fusion helps, the many multimodal configurations become worth exploring further, for example with weighted fusion, ViT-L or the transformer aggregation option. If it does not, the budget can shift to RNA-side choices such as the scVI or scGPT encoders and transformer aggregation in RNA-only models. Under a limited budget, this is the most informative single comparison available.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 added a resnet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (multiprofile, avgpool, pca_n2000) from llm_summary_002, testing whether images add complementary signal despite their weak standalone result (0.3275 acc in llm_summary_003). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6186 (F1 0.6103), a modest gain over RNA-only multiprofile (0.5907 acc, +0.028; F1 0.5727, +0.038), and the F1-accuracy gap narrowed to about 0.008. This is initial evidence that adding resnet50 image features via concat fusion helps rather than degrades performance, which tentatively supports further multimodal exploration. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so a gain of about 0.03 may not be reliable, and it remains untested whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), transformer aggregation, or stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would enlarge, preserve, or erase this benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The largest observed gain came from switching to multiprofile with avgpool (+0.106 accuracy in RNA-only). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion gave a further modest gain, reaching the current best (config_018: 0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1). Aggregation has only ever been avgpool, so we do not know how much of the multiprofile benefit depends on the pooling choice. 2) Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else in config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat). This isolates whether learned set aggregation adds to the strongest direction found so far. 3) Why now: Aggregation is a core design choice tied to the most impactful axis observed. A one-change comparison against the current best is both a direct exploit and an informative test. A null or negative result would also be useful, since it would tell us to keep simple pooling and focus remaining budget on RNA encoders, image encoders or fusion. With single runs, a small difference should be read cautiously, using F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the aggregation of the current best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) from avgpool to transformer, to test whether learned set aggregation adds to the strongest direction found so far. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6186 to 0.5793 (-0.039), and validation F1 fell in parallel from 0.6103 to 0.5631 (-0.047). Both values are also slightly below the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool run (0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1), and the F1-accuracy gap widened again to about 0.016. Because this was a clean one-change comparison, the drop is attributable to the aggregation switch in this setup, which tentatively favors keeping avgpool and spending remaining budget on RNA encoders, image encoders, or fusion. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size and reliability of the drop are uncertain. It also remains untested whether transformer aggregation underperforms due to its training or hyperparameters (it may need more data or tuning), or whether it would behave differently with RNA-only input, other encoders, or other fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591 accuracy, while image-only reached 0.328. Adding resnet50 with concat fusion gave a modest further gain to 0.619 (config_018, current best). Transformer aggregation hurt (0.579), so avgpool is the working choice for now. The RNA encoder has never been varied: every RNA run so far used pca_n2000. Given how much of the performance comes from RNA, this is the largest untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_042 changes only the RNA encoder of the best configuration, from pca_n2000 to scGPT. Profile setting (multiprofile), image encoder (resnet50), aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) stay fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation within the strongest pipeline found so far. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it combines exploitation (it extends the best configuration) with exploration (it reduces uncertainty on the axis most likely to matter). Weighted fusion or ViT-L image encoders act on the weaker image contribution and seem likely to produce smaller changes. Whether scGPT helps or hurts, the result will tell us whether later experiments should stay with PCA or move to learned or pretrained RNA encoders. scVI can follow as the complementary comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder of the current best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat), replacing pca_n2000 with scGPT, which was the first test of the RNA encoder axis. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.6186 to 0.5121 (-0.107), and F1 fell further from 0.6103 to 0.4771 (-0.133), widening the F1-accuracy gap to about 0.035. The result is below RNA-only PCA multiprofile (0.5907), only slightly above the singleprofile PCA baseline (0.4849), and well above image-only (0.3275). Because this was a clean one-change comparison, the drop is attributable to the scGPT swap in this pipeline, which tentatively favors keeping pca_n2000.
