The size of the drop is still uncertain because each configuration has a single run with unknown run-to-run variance. It also remains unknown whether scGPT underperforms because of how its embeddings were extracted, frozen, or fine-tuned, or because of how it interacts with concat fusion and avgpool, and neither RNA-only scGPT nor scVI has been tested yet.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat), with 0.6186 accuracy and 0.6103 F1. Two one-change tests from it both lowered performance: switching to transformer aggregation and switching to the scGPT RNA encoder. Adding resnet50 images helped only modestly (+0.028 accuracy), and resnet50 alone was weak (0.3275). The image branch may therefore be the bottleneck, and the image-encoder axis has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_024 changes only the image encoder of config_018, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal to PCA RNA features. It also helps show whether the weak image results reflect the image modality itself or the resnet50 pipeline. 3. Why now: This is a clean single-change comparison on the strongest configuration, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Untested axes remain: image encoder, fusion (weighted) and scVI. The image encoder is the most likely lever, because the image branch is clearly the weaker component. The weighted fusion and scVI comparisons can follow depending on this result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the image encoder of the previous best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat), replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l. This was the first test of the image-encoder axis, meant to check whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal to PCA RNA features. Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.6186 to 0.6287 (+0.010), making this the best accuracy so far, but validation F1 fell from 0.6103 to 0.5993 (-0.011), widening the F1-accuracy gap from about 0.008 to about 0.029. The accuracy gain may come with less even per-class performance, but this is unconfirmed without per-class results. Because the accuracy and F1 changes are small and point in opposite directions, and each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, this is at most weak evidence that ViT-L helps. It is still untested whether ViT-L images are stronger on their own (no image-only ViT-L run exists), whether weighted fusion or scVI would add to this setup, and whether the F1 drop reflects a real tradeoff or noise.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal source (RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only 0.328). The RNA encoder axis has the largest effect seen so far: swapping PCA for scGPT cost about 0.107 accuracy and 0.133 F1. scVI, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. The current best configuration is config_024 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.629 accuracy). 2) Test: this run changes only the RNA encoder of config_024, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. It shows whether PCA is genuinely the best RNA representation or whether scGPT was a specific failure, and whether scVI's compact latent space combines better with image features. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder axis has shown large effects, so this test can move accuracy far more than the remaining untested axis, fusion (concat vs weighted), which is likely to give smaller, noise-level differences. It is a clean one-change comparison against the current best, so it serves both exploration (an untested encoder) and exploitation (the best surrounding setup). Weighted fusion is a good candidate for a later run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the RNA encoder of the previous best configuration (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat), replacing pca_n2000 with scvi_n200, the first test of scVI. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6287 to 0.7150 (+0.086), the best so far by a wide margin, and F1 rose in parallel from 0.5993 to 0.6872 (+0.088), with the F1-accuracy gap staying at about 0.028. Because this was a clean one-change comparison, the gain is attributable to the scVI swap in this ViT-L pipeline. Together with the scGPT drop in llm_summary_006, this reinforces that the RNA encoder is the largest-effect axis found so far and suggests PCA is not the best RNA representation. The swap changed both the method (scVI vs PCA) and the dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so the two cannot be separated. It also remains uncertain how large the gain truly is (single runs, unknown variance), whether scVI helps as much in RNA-only or resnet50 setups (its interaction with ViT-L is untested), and whether weighted fusion would add further gains on top of this new best.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the current best is config_036 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. The RNA encoder has been the largest-effect axis, avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. Fusion is the only major design axis never tested: every multimodal run so far used concat, so whether weighted fusion helps is completely unknown. 2) Test: config_037 changes only concat to weighted on the best configuration. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion method in the strongest pipeline. Weighted fusion could also matter more now, because scVI and ViT-L may contribute unequally. 3) Value: this one experiment probes an entirely unexplored axis and also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. The main alternative, RNA-only scVI (config_005), is a good candidate for later to check whether images still add value over scVI.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method of the current best configuration (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool), replacing concat with weighted fusion. This was the first test of the fusion axis, since all earlier multimodal runs used concat. Validation accuracy fell slightly from 0.7150 to 0.7062 (-0.009), and F1 fell more, from 0.6872 to 0.6671 (-0.020), widening the F1-accuracy gap from about 0.028 to about 0.039. In this single clean one-change comparison, weighted fusion did not beat concat in the strongest pipeline and gave slightly worse results, so llm_summary_008 remains the best. The accuracy difference is small, though, and with single runs and unknown run-to-run variance it may be noise. It remains untested whether weighted fusion behaves differently with other encoders (e.g., PCA or resnet50) or with tuning, whether the wider F1 gap reflects a real per-class tradeoff, and whether images still add value over RNA-only scVI.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_036 (multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Swapping the RNA encoder was the largest effect seen: scVI gave +0.086 and scGPT gave -0.107. Image changes gave much smaller effects: adding resnet50 gave +0.028, ViT-L gave +0.010 in accuracy with lower F1, and weighted fusion did slightly worse than concat. So most of the gain may come from scVI alone. We do not know whether images still add anything once the RNA representation is strong. 2. What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile and avgpool. It is a clean one-change ablation of the best configuration, since it only removes the image branch. It also directly compares scVI with PCA in the RNA-only multiprofile setting (0.591), which shows whether the scVI gain depends on ViT-L. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, it matters more to know whether multimodality is worth its cost than to tune further multimodal variants. If RNA-only scVI comes close to 0.715, later effort should go to the RNA side. If it falls clearly short, that confirms images add complementary signal and justifies more image and fusion tuning.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 removed the image branch and fusion from the current best configuration (llm_summary_008: multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat), giving an RNA-only scVI multiprofile avgpool model; it also served as a one-change RNA-encoder comparison against RNA-only PCA multiprofile (llm_summary_002). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (F1 0.6275). That is 0.065 below the multimodal scVI+ViT-L best (0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1) but 0.059 above RNA-only PCA (0.5907 acc, 0.5727 F1), with an F1-accuracy gap of about 0.023. This suggests that scVI's advantage over PCA does not depend on ViT-L, and that images still add complementary signal on top of a strong RNA representation; the image gain here (+0.065) appears larger than with PCA RNA (+0.028 to +0.038), hinting at a possible positive scVI-image interaction. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, scVI's method and dimensionality (200 vs 2000) are confounded, scVI with resnet50 and image-only ViT-L are untested, and it is unclear whether further image or fusion tuning or RNA-side improvements would give larger gains.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline for accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against. From here, single-factor changes are easy to isolate: encoder (scVI or scGPT, configs 004 and 007), profile setting and aggregation (configs 002 and 003), and modality (image-only or multimodal). 3) Why now: With a limited budget, anchoring the search with a cheap, interpretable baseline is the most efficient first step. It lets us judge whether more complex multiprofile or multimodal models actually add value, rather than assuming they do.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder, no image encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 (validation F1 0.464), which serves as an initial reference baseline. No other experiments have been completed, so it is not yet known whether this level is good or poor, or which factor (RNA encoder, profile setting/aggregation, or adding the image modality) would most improve on it. Single-factor changes from this baseline, such as swapping in scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or image/multimodal settings, are needed to tell whether added complexity helps, and run-to-run variance is also not yet characterized.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.485 and F1 0.464. We do not yet know which design axis matters most. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping RNA-only and the PCA encoder fixed. This isolates whether pooling over multiple profiles helps over single profiles. 3) Why now: the profile-setting question affects every branch of the search space (RNA, image and multimodal configurations alike), so answering it early tells us how to read later experiments. Avgpool is the simplest multiprofile option, so it gives a clean comparison before testing transformer aggregation, other encoders or added modalities. An encoder swap (config_004) would also be a clean single-factor test, but its answer mainly applies to RNA encoders.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only model with the PCA (2000-component) encoder, switching from single-profile to multiprofile input with average-pooling aggregation; this is the only change from the llm_summary_001 baseline. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591 (about +0.106), and validation F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, which suggests that pooling over multiple profiles helps in this RNA-only PCA setting. This rests on one run per configuration with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, so the size of the gain, and possibly whether it holds up, is uncertain. Several questions remain untested: whether the benefit carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only or multimodal settings, or richer aggregation such as transformer pooling, and whether it comes from multiprofile information itself or from the avgpool choice specifically.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far only RNA-only PCA models have been run. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose in line. This rests on one run each, but it makes multiprofile avgpool the best reference so far. Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though most of the search space (all image-only and multimodal configurations) depends on it. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the best profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the modality, from the RNA PCA encoder to the ResNet50 image encoder. This shows how much signal images carry on their own, compared directly with config_002. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Whether images are informative is the largest open question, and it decides whether the many multimodal and image configurations deserve budget. Aggregation (config_003) and RNA encoder (config_005) comparisons can follow once the value of the image modality is known.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an image-only model with a ResNet50 image encoder and multiprofile avgpool aggregation, with no RNA encoder and no fusion. It differs from llm_summary_002 only in modality, swapping the RNA PCA encoder for ResNet50 images. It reached validation accuracy 0.328 (F1 0.288), far below the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.591 / 0.573) and also below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is an initial observation that, in this setup, ResNet50 image features alone carry much less class signal than RNA PCA features. It rests on one run with uncharacterized variance, and it remains unknown whether images add complementary value in multimodal fusion, whether other image encoders or aggregation methods would do better, and whether multiprofile pooling helps the image modality at all, since no single-profile image run exists for comparison.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool improved the RNA-only PCA model from 0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, the best result so far. ResNet50 image-only with the same aggregation reached only 0.328. Whether images add complementary signal on top of RNA is the central untested question for multimodal profiling. A weak unimodal result does not rule out a benefit from fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best RNA setup (PCA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 images with simple concat fusion. It is a near single-factor comparison against config_002, isolating the effect of adding the image modality. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The result decides whether the many remaining multimodal configurations are worth exploring. If fusion does not beat 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1, the budget should shift toward RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation (transformer) comparisons. If it helps, fusion variants and stronger image encoders become the priority.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested a multimodal model that adds ResNet50 image features, combined by simple concat fusion, to the best RNA setup so far (PCA n2000 encoder, multiprofile, avgpool). It is a near single-factor comparison against llm_summary_002 (RNA-only, same settings). Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.619 (about +0.028) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.610 (about +0.038), the best result so far. This is an initial indication that images add some complementary signal to RNA despite the weak image-only result (0.328 / 0.288). Each configuration has one run and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so the modest gain may be partly noise. It is also untested whether the benefit holds with other fusion methods, stronger image encoders, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or other aggregation such as transformer pooling, and whether it comes from the image content itself or from the added input dimensionality and capacity.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA carries most of the class signal. RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591, image-only reached 0.328, and adding images gave a modest +0.028 (0.619). Multiprofile avgpool also clearly helped PCA (+0.106). However, every result so far uses the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the effect of RNA representation is completely unknown. Because RNA dominates performance, it is plausibly the highest-impact factor. 2. What this tests: config_008 differs from config_002 only in the RNA encoder (scGPT instead of PCA), keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats PCA and shows whether the multiprofile setup carries over to another encoder. 3. Why it is the best next step: other open questions (weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, ViT-L images) target factors that so far showed smaller effects or act through the weaker image modality. Testing the RNA encoder in the clean RNA-only setting avoids confounding it with fusion. Its result will guide which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal experiments, whether scGPT wins or loses.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool model using the pretrained scGPT RNA encoder. It differs from llm_summary_002 only in the RNA encoder (scGPT instead of PCA n2000). Validation accuracy was 0.530 (F1 0.515), about 0.060 below the PCA counterpart (0.591 / 0.573) but above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464), so in this setup scGPT embeddings with avgpool give an initial indication of weaker class signal than PCA features. Each configuration has one run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance. It is unknown whether the gap reflects the representation itself or how well scGPT embeddings suit avgpool and the downstream head. Multiprofile pooling cannot be credited for scGPT's gap above the PCA single-profile baseline, because no single-profile scGPT run exists and that comparison differs in two factors. scVI remains untested, and scGPT's behavior in multimodal fusion is also unknown, so PCA remains the stronger RNA choice for now but the encoder question is not settled.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool gave the largest gain so far (+0.106 accuracy, 0.485 to 0.591, in RNA-only PCA). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a smaller gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). PCA beat scGPT. However, avgpool is the only aggregation tested, so we do not know whether the multiprofile gain comes from multiprofile information itself or is limited by the simple pooling choice. 2) Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and PCA n2000, so it is a clean single-factor comparison with config_002 (0.591 / 0.573). It shows whether learned attention over profiles extracts more signal than mean pooling. 3) Value: Aggregation applies to nearly every remaining multiprofile configuration, whether RNA-only, image-only or multimodal. Settling it in the cheapest, strongest-signal modality guides many later choices, more than a fusion or image-encoder swap, which so far has shown a smaller effect. scVI (config_005) is a strong next candidate for the encoder question afterward.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA n2000 encoder and transformer aggregation. It is a clean single-factor comparison with llm_summary_002, changing only avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 (about -0.072) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.480, which places it only slightly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is an initial indication that, in this setup, transformer aggregation does worse than simple mean pooling, and avgpool remains the preferred aggregation for now. Each configuration has only one run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the transformer's training details, capacity and tuning are unknown. It is therefore unclear whether the drop reflects attention-based aggregation itself or under-tuning or overfitting of a higher-capacity aggregator. It is also unknown whether the result carries over to image-only, multimodal, or other RNA-encoder (scVI, scGPT) settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA reached 0.591 accuracy, against 0.328 for image-only ResNet50. Adding images gave only a modest gain, 0.619 for config_018. Among RNA encoders, PCA beat scGPT (0.591 vs 0.530), but scVI, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200 relative to config_002, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This cleanly shows whether scVI's lower-dimensional latent representation beats, matches or trails PCA. 3. Why this is the best next use: RNA drives most of the performance, so settling the RNA representation affects every downstream multimodal configuration. If scVI wins, it should be carried into fusion runs; if it loses, PCA is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to image-encoder (ViT-L) and fusion-method comparisons around config_018. A one-factor test on the dominant modality is more informative now than tuning the weaker image branch or the fusion method.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool model with the scVI (200-dimensional latent) RNA encoder, a clean single-factor comparison with llm_summary_002 that swaps only PCA n2000 for scVI n200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 (about +0.059) and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628. This is the best result so far, ahead of the scGPT RNA-only run (0.530 / 0.515) and also the PCA+ResNet50 concat multimodal run (0.619 / 0.610), although that last comparison differs in several factors. It is an initial indication that scVI is the strongest RNA encoder in this setup, but each configuration has one run with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the encoder swap also changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so the result cannot be credited to the scVI model itself versus its lower-dimensional representation. It also remains untested whether scVI's advantage holds in multimodal fusion with images, so scVI-based multimodal runs are a natural next check.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI n200 is the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1, RNA-only multiprofile avgpool). Multiprofile avgpool beat both single-profile and transformer aggregation with PCA. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a modest gain over PCA RNA-only (0.591 to 0.619). Each result is a single run, and it is unknown whether the image gain carries over to a stronger RNA representation. 2) config_030 changes only one factor from config_005 (adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion to scVI multiprofile avgpool). It also mirrors the PCA comparison (config_002 vs config_018). The run tests whether images still add complementary signal when RNA features are stronger, or whether that gain disappears. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the current best direction and has a good chance of producing the top configuration. It also clarifies whether multimodal fusion is worth exploring further, for example weighted fusion or ViT-L. That makes it more decision-relevant than retesting aggregations or encoders that have already performed weakly.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 tested a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool model that adds ResNet50 image features via concat fusion to the scVI n200 RNA encoder. It is a clean single-factor comparison with the current best run, llm_summary_007 (RNA-only scVI, same settings). Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.632 (about -0.019) and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607 (about -0.021), which contrasts with the PCA setting, where adding images with concat raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.619 (llm_summary_002 vs 004). This run still ranks second overall, slightly above the PCA multimodal run, but it gives an initial indication that the complementary image gain does not carry over once the RNA representation is stronger, and RNA-only scVI remains the best configuration. All results are single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and both the earlier gain and this drop are small, so either could be noise. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects redundant image signal, or the concat design with a low-dimensional (200-d) RNA input next to image features. Other fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion), stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or tuning could change the picture, so the value of multimodal fusion with scVI is not settled.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI multiprofile avgpool is the best run (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion lowered it slightly (0.632 / 0.607). With PCA, the same concat addition helped (0.591 to 0.619). So whether images add value depends on the RNA encoder, and the concat design may be the limiting factor. A plausible cause is that weak image features (image-only 0.328) dilute a compact 200-d scVI input under concat. 2) Test: config_031 keeps everything from config_030 (scVI n200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of the fusion method. If weighted fusion lets the model down-weight the image branch and matches or beats 0.650, multimodal fusion stays viable on top of scVI. If it still falls below RNA-only scVI, that strengthens the view that ResNet50 images are redundant once RNA is strong. 3) Why now: fusion method is the remaining untested major design axis. This clean single-factor comparison is built on the current best setup, so it serves both exploitation (a chance to beat 0.650) and uncertainty reduction. It also tells us whether weighted fusion is worth carrying into later image-encoder tests (e.g., ViT-L) rather than changing several factors at once.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 tested a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool model with scVI n200 RNA and ResNet50 image encoders using weighted fusion. It is a clean single-factor comparison with llm_summary_008, which used concat fusion with otherwise identical settings. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.678 (about +0.046) and F1 from 0.607 to 0.646. This is the best result so far, ahead of RNA-only scVI (0.650 / 0.628), so it gives an initial indication that weighted fusion can recover and exceed the RNA-only result where concat did not, and that multimodal fusion on top of scVI remains viable. All results are single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the margin over RNA-only scVI is modest (about +0.028 accuracy, +0.019 F1). It is also unknown whether the gain comes from complementary image signal, from the weighting mechanism down-weighting the image branch, or from extra fusion parameters and capacity, and whether weighted fusion helps with PCA, scGPT, or stronger image encoders such as ViT-L.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). It uses scVI n200, multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion. scVI was the strongest RNA encoder, avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion beat concat. The image encoder has never been varied, and ResNet50 was weak on its own (0.328 image-only). So it is unclear whether a better image representation would add more complementary signal. 2. What this tests: config_037 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps every other part of the best setup. This isolates the effect of image representation quality inside weighted fusion. It also helps show whether config_031's gain over RNA-only scVI comes from real image signal or mainly from the weighting reducing the image branch's influence. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it can improve on the best result. At the same time, it fills the largest untested design dimension, which affects many of the remaining configurations. The result will show whether later runs should invest in ViT-L or stay with ResNet50. Since all results are single runs, a small difference either way should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested a multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool model with scVI n200 RNA, weighted fusion and an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder; it is a clean single-factor comparison with the previous best, llm_summary_009, changing only ResNet50 to ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.706 (about +0.029) and F1 from 0.646 to 0.667 (about +0.021), making this the best result so far and well above RNA-only scVI (0.650 / 0.628), which gives an initial indication that a stronger image representation adds complementary signal within weighted fusion. All results are single runs with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, so the modest margin is suggestive rather than conclusive. It is still unknown how ViT-L performs image-only, with concat fusion, or with other RNA encoders. It is also unclear whether the gain reflects better image features specifically or other differences between the encoders, such as embedding dimensionality, and how the fusion weights treat the image branch.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about how well any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice performs on this task. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration, RNA-only and single-profile with PCA (2000 components) and no aggregation or fusion. It gives a low-complexity reference accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: scVI or scGPT encoders (config_004, config_007), multiprofile aggregation (config_002, config_003), the image modality (config_010), and fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting with a simple baseline avoids changing several design choices at once. It lets us judge whether added complexity (learned encoders, multiprofile, multimodal) actually helps, rather than assuming it does. It also shows early whether the task is easy or hard, which helps plan the remaining budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 ran the simplest configuration as a baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, a PCA RNA encoder with 2000 components, no image encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485 and a validation F1 of 0.464, so it misclassifies about half of validation samples. The close F1 suggests performance is not strongly skewed toward a few classes, though this is inferred only from the two aggregate metrics. Because no other experiments have been completed and the number of classes and chance level are not given, this is only an initial reference point: it does not show whether learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would help, and run-to-run variance is unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). Every other design axis is untested, and run-to-run variance is unknown. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed and switches to multiprofile input with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of the profile setting. A clear gain would mean pooling information across profiles matters, which would justify trying transformer aggregation and multiprofile variants of other encoders and modalities. No gain would mean single-profile configurations deserve more of the budget. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Profile setting is shared across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings, so its answer shapes much of the remaining search space. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity way to probe it, so any change is attributable to adding profiles rather than to a complex aggregator. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and the image-only baseline are natural follow-ups once this axis is understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_001 but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, combining profiles with mean pooling (avgpool) and using no image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 and F1 of 0.573, about 0.106 and 0.109 above the single-profile baseline (0.485 and 0.464). This suggests that combining information across profiles may help in this RNA-only PCA setting, and the close F1 again suggests the gain is not confined to a few classes. The evidence is limited: it is one run per configuration with unknown run-to-run variance, avgpool is the only aggregator tested, and it is unknown whether the gain holds for learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the image modality, multimodal fusion, or stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only RNA-only PCA runs exist. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with F1 rising in step (0.464 to 0.573). The image modality, however, is completely untested, and it underlies more than half of the remaining search space (all image-only and multimodal configurations). 2. Test: Running image-only ResNet50 with the same multiprofile avgpool setup as the best run (config_002) changes only the modality, while profile setting and aggregation stay fixed. It shows how informative images are on their own and whether the multiprofile setup behaves similarly outside RNA. 3. Why now: Knowing whether images are weak, comparable or stronger than RNA PCA is the biggest uncertainty for deciding whether to spend later budget on multimodal fusion or focus on RNA encoders and aggregators. That makes this more informative now than a small tweak to the RNA aggregator or encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the image modality for the first time: image-only, multiprofile, with a ResNet50 image encoder and avgpool aggregation, no RNA encoder and no fusion. It matched llm_summary_002 (RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile avgpool) except for modality. It reached validation accuracy 0.328 and F1 0.288, well below the RNA-only multiprofile run (0.591 / 0.573) and the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.485 / 0.464). This is an initial observation that ResNet50 image features with avgpool appear weaker than PCA RNA features in this setup. The F1–accuracy gap (~0.04, slightly wider than in RNA runs) may hint at less even performance across classes, though this is inferred only from aggregate metrics. It remains uncertain whether the weakness reflects image informativeness in general or this specific encoder/aggregation choice, since no single-profile image run, other image encoders, or other aggregators have been tested. It is also untested whether images add complementary signal under multimodal fusion despite weak standalone performance. Each configuration has one run, run-to-run variance is unknown, and chance level is not given.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: multiprofile avgpool improved RNA-only PCA-2000 from 0.485 to 0.591 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 under the same multiprofile avgpool setting was much weaker (0.328 accuracy). Every result is a single run with unknown variance. The study's central untested question is whether the image modality adds complementary signal when fused with RNA, even though images are weak on their own. 2) config_018 is config_002 plus ResNet50 image features combined by concat fusion. Profile setting, aggregation and RNA encoder stay the same. It also matches config_011 except for adding RNA. Accuracy and F1 relative to 0.591/0.573 will show whether fusion helps, does nothing, or hurts, as weak image features can add noise. 3) This is the best next experiment because the answer decides how much of the remaining budget should go to the many multimodal configurations. A clear gain would justify exploring fusion types and image encoders. No gain or a drop would point the budget toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation (transformer) in RNA-only models. Concat is the simpler fusion baseline and should be tested before weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 is the first multimodal run: RNA PCA-2000 plus ResNet50 image features, multiprofile avgpool aggregation, and concat fusion. It differs from the RNA-only multiprofile run (llm_summary_002) only by adding the image modality, and it reached validation accuracy 0.619 and F1 0.610, about +0.028 accuracy and +0.038 F1 over that run (0.591 / 0.573) and far above image-only (0.328 / 0.288). This is an initial sign that weak standalone image features may add complementary signal when concatenated with RNA rather than only adding noise, and the narrower F1–accuracy gap (~0.008) may hint at more even per-class performance, though this is inferred only from aggregate metrics. The gain is modest and comes from single runs with unknown variance, so it may lie within run-to-run noise. It is also untested whether the benefit holds for other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), image encoders, learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_002) reached 0.591 accuracy, versus 0.328 for image-only. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave only a modest gain (0.619), which may lie within run-to-run noise. Multiprofile avgpool also appears to help over single-profile (+0.106). However, every run so far uses PCA-2000 for RNA. The RNA encoder is therefore a completely untested design axis, and it controls the strongest signal source. 2. What this tests: config_005 is identical to config_002 except that it swaps PCA-2000 for scVI-200. This isolates whether a learned probabilistic RNA representation beats PCA, with profile setting, aggregation, modality and fusion held fixed. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: because RNA carries most of the predictive signal, the RNA encoder choice is likely to matter more than secondary choices such as fusion type or image encoder. The answer also directly shapes which part of the large multimodal grid (configs 030–039 versus 042–051) is worth exploring. Testing it in the RNA-only setting avoids confounding with image or fusion effects while staying close to the current best-performing direction.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was identical to llm_summary_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) except that it replaced the PCA-2000 RNA encoder with a learned scVI encoder with 200 latent dimensions, so it isolates the RNA encoder choice within this setting. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 and F1 0.628, about +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over the PCA-2000 counterpart (0.591 / 0.573). It also exceeded the multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 concat run (0.619 / 0.610), making it the best result so far. This is initial evidence that scVI-200 may be a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 here, though the F1–accuracy gap (~0.023) is wider than in the multimodal run, which may hint at less even per-class performance (inferred only from aggregate metrics). Each configuration has a single run and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the gain's robustness is uncertain. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds in single-profile or multimodal settings with image fusion, under other aggregators, or relative to scGPT, and whether it comes from the learned probabilistic model or from the different dimensionality (200 vs 2000) cannot be separated.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Two single-run findings point in promising directions within the multiprofile avgpool setting. Replacing PCA-2000 with scVI-200 improved accuracy by about 0.059 (0.591 to 0.650), the best result so far. Separately, adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion to PCA-2000 improved accuracy by about 0.028 (0.591 to 0.619), with a narrower F1 gap. It is unknown whether the image gain holds once the RNA representation is stronger. It could be additive, or it could be redundant with what scVI already captures. 2. Test: config_030 combines scVI-200 and ResNet50 images with multiprofile avgpool and concat fusion. It differs from config_005 only by adding images, which tests whether images still help on top of scVI. It differs from config_018 only by the RNA encoder, which tests whether scVI's advantage carries into the multimodal setting. 3. Why now: It is one experiment that gives two clean single-factor comparisons. It is also the most likely next new best, so it balances exploitation with resolving the key modality-complementarity question before spending budget on untested axes. Those axes, transformer aggregation, scGPT and ViT-L, can then be explored around a stronger base configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 combined scVI-200 RNA features with ResNet50 image features (multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion), giving two single-factor comparisons: it differs from llm_summary_005 (RNA-only scVI-200, 0.650 / 0.628) only by adding images, and from llm_summary_004 (multimodal PCA-2000, 0.619 / 0.610) only by the RNA encoder. It reached validation accuracy 0.632 and F1 0.607, about −0.019 accuracy and −0.021 F1 below RNA-only scVI. Relative to multimodal PCA-2000 it was +0.013 accuracy but −0.004 F1, and its F1–accuracy gap (~0.025) did not show the narrower gap seen in llm_summary_004. This is an initial observation that the modest image gain seen with PCA (+0.028) may not carry over once RNA is encoded with scVI, and that scVI's advantage over PCA appears smaller in this multimodal concat setting. However, all differences come from single runs with unknown run-to-run variance and may lie within noise. It remains untested whether a different fusion method (e.g., weighted), feature scaling or dimensionality balance between modalities (200-dim scVI vs 2048-dim ResNet50 under concat), other image encoders (ViT-L), or transformer aggregation would change whether images add complementary or redundant signal; llm_summary_005 remains the best result so far.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: multiprofile input gave the largest gain so far (+0.106 accuracy for PCA). scVI-200 beat PCA-2000 (+0.059), and RNA-only scVI with avgpool is the current best (0.650 / 0.628). Adding ResNet50 images through concat helped with PCA but not with scVI. Only avgpool has ever been tested, so aggregation is a completely unexplored design axis, even though profile combination is the strongest effect observed. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It isolates whether a learned aggregator extracts more from multiple profiles than mean pooling. 3) It exploits the strongest direction while answering an open question that affects every multiprofile configuration, including later multimodal ones. It is a cleaner and more broadly informative next step than testing weighted fusion or scGPT, since the aggregation result will guide the setup for those later comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 took the best configuration so far (llm_summary_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI-200) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer, isolating aggregation for the first time. It reached validation accuracy 0.653 and F1 0.628, essentially tied with avgpool (0.650 / 0.628): +0.003 accuracy and +0.001 F1, with a similar F1–accuracy gap (~0.025). It is nominally the best result so far, but this is an initial observation that learned transformer aggregation gives little or no measurable benefit over mean pooling here, and the margin likely lies within run-to-run noise, which is unknown because each configuration has a single run. It remains untested whether a transformer aggregator would matter more with PCA-2000 features, in multimodal settings with ResNet50 concat or weighted fusion, with other encoders (scGPT, ViT-L), or under different transformer hyperparameters, so avgpool and transformer should currently be treated as roughly equivalent for RNA-only scVI multiprofile input.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder has been the largest single-factor lever after profile setting. Swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 gave about +0.059 accuracy in the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting. Aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) made almost no difference. Adding ResNet50 images helped slightly with PCA but not with scVI. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested, so a major axis of the design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_008 matches config_005 (scVI-200, 0.650/0.628) and config_002 (PCA-2000, 0.591/0.573) except for the RNA encoder. It therefore directly shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats or falls short of scVI. It uses avgpool, which performed about the same as the transformer at lower complexity. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: The result will decide which RNA encoder anchors all later multimodal, fusion and aggregation experiments, and most remaining configurations depend on that choice. Testing fusion variants such as weighted fusion before knowing the best RNA representation risks spending budget on a weaker backbone. The run is also a plausible candidate for a new best accuracy, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested scGPT, the third RNA encoder and the only one not yet tried, in the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting. This makes it a single-factor comparison with llm_summary_005 (scVI-200, 0.650 / 0.628) and llm_summary_002 (PCA-2000, 0.591 / 0.573). It reached validation accuracy 0.530 and F1 0.515, about −0.120 accuracy below scVI-200 and −0.060 below PCA-2000, and only modestly above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485). This is initial evidence that, as configured here, scGPT embeddings are the weakest of the three RNA representations, and scVI-200 remains the leading RNA encoder (best overall: llm_summary_007, 0.653, with llm_summary_005 essentially tied). The gap is large relative to the other observed differences, but each configuration has a single run with unknown variance. It also remains untested whether scGPT's weakness reflects the representation itself or how it was extracted or adapted (e.g., frozen vs fine-tuned, embedding dimensionality, gene vocabulary overlap), and whether it would behave differently under transformer aggregation, single-profile input, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI-200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, and transformer aggregation is roughly tied with avgpool (0.653 vs 0.650). Adding ResNet50 images by concat helped with PCA (+0.028) but hurt with scVI (0.632 vs 0.650). One possible cause is imbalance under concat, with 200-dim scVI features next to 2048-dim image features. Fusion method has not been varied at all. 2) Test: config_031 changes only concat to weighted fusion relative to config_030 (scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the fusion choice and shows whether images can add complementary signal on top of the best RNA encoder, or whether they are redundant or noisy. 3) Value: whether multimodality is worth pursuing is the most decision-relevant open question, and fusion is a completely untested design axis. A single-factor comparison against an existing run tells us whether to keep exploring multimodal configurations (including ViT-L) or to focus on RNA-only scVI. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept llm_summary_006 fixed (multimodal scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, so it isolates fusion for the first time. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 and F1 0.646, which is +0.046 accuracy and +0.040 F1 over concat (0.632 / 0.607) and about +0.025 to +0.027 accuracy over the RNA-only scVI runs (0.650 avgpool, 0.653 transformer), making it the best result so far. This is initial evidence that, with scVI-200 RNA features, weighted fusion lets ResNet50 images add complementary signal, whereas concat did not. The F1–accuracy gap (~0.031) is slightly wider than in the RNA-only scVI runs, which may hint at less even per-class performance, though this is inferred only from aggregate metrics. Each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, so the margins may partly reflect noise. The mechanism is also unconfirmed: the result fits, but does not prove, the hypothesis that concat suffered from imbalance between 200-dim scVI and 2048-dim image features. It also remains untested whether weighted fusion helps with PCA-2000 or scGPT, with ViT-L images, or with transformer aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). Weighted fusion appears to let image features add signal on top of RNA-only scVI (0.650–0.653), while concat did not. The image encoder is the one major design choice not yet tested: every image run so far has used ResNet50, and ResNet50 alone was weak (0.328). So it is unclear whether image features are inherently limited here or whether ResNet50 is the bottleneck. 2) What this tests: config_037 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the complementary image contribution under weighted fusion. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It is a single-factor test of an untested dimension, so it is informative whatever the outcome. It also builds directly on the strongest current configuration, so it has a good chance of improving the best result. Transformer aggregation (config_033) is a less useful next step because it showed no measurable benefit in the RNA-only setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the previous best configuration (llm_summary_009: multimodal scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) fixed and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, the first test of a non-ResNet50 image encoder. It reached validation accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667, about +0.029 accuracy and +0.021 F1 over the ResNet50 counterpart (0.678 / 0.646) and about +0.053 to +0.056 accuracy over the RNA-only scVI runs (0.650–0.653), making it the best result so far. This is initial evidence that ResNet50 was at least partly limiting the image contribution, and that a stronger image representation can add more complementary signal under weighted fusion, although the F1–accuracy gap widened slightly (~0.039 vs ~0.031), which may hint at less even per-class performance (inferred only from aggregate metrics). Each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, so the margin may partly reflect noise. It also remains untested how ViT-L performs image-only or under concat fusion, whether its benefit comes from architecture, model size, or feature dimensionality, and whether it interacts with transformer aggregation or other RNA encoders (PCA-2000, scGPT).
